item.title: Coinbase Launches U.S. Spot Margin Trading With Up to 10x Leverage
item.description: Bitcoin Magazine Coinbase Launches U.S. Spot Margin Trading With Up to 10x Leverage Coinbase (COIN) has opened crypto spot margin trading to U.S. customers, letting eligible traders borrow to go long or short with up to 10x leverage, the exchange announced Wednesday, though access is limited to investors with more than $10 million invested. “Crypto spot margin is now available in the US for eligible traders,” Coinbase wrote on X. Traders borrow at the moment they place an order, rather than setting up a loan first. The eligibility bar is high. In a follow-up post , Coinbase said margin trading is open only to people who qualify as “eligible contract participants” under the Commodity Exchange Act. For an individual, that generally means more than $10 million in assets invested on a discretionary basis. The product is also not available in all states, and the loans are for commercial or business purposes only, the company said. Coinbase did not list eligible states or assets in the posts. The limit tracks how U.S. law treats leverage. Under the Commodity Exchange Act , leveraged retail commodity trades generally have to run through a regulated futures exchange, so off-exchange margin products like this one are often reserved for eligible contract participants. How spot margin works Coinbase first described spot margin in October. Eligible traders can borrow against collateral to increase their buying power on spot markets, with leverage of up to 10x on selected major assets and up to 5x on other supported assets. Collateral can be posted in more than 15 supported assets and stays on Coinbase throughout. Loan balances, collateral levels and margin health appear in real time, and spot positions sit in the same margin portfolio as a trader’s derivatives. For U.S. customers, Coinbase Credit, Inc. makes the loans and Coinbase, Inc. holds the collateral as custodian. The company said spot margin is not a product of Coinbase Financial Markets, its regulated U.S. futures broker. The risk disclosures are blunt. Variable-rate interest accrues hourly and can erode a trader’s margin level, and market moves can trigger margin calls or automatic liquidation. In October, the company warned that collateral “may be liquidated without notice” and that traders can lose more than their initial deposit. Part of a bigger trading push from Coinbase Spot margin is one piece of what Coinbase calls its “Everything Exchange.” In the same October post, it said its integration of Deribit was complete and that crypto options, spot margin and unified portfolios would roll out in the coming weeks. That push leans on guidance the Commodity Futures Trading Commission issued in May, which Coinbase said made Coinbase Financial Markets the only U.S. futures commission merchant able to connect U.S. clients to global crypto derivatives liquidity. The CFTC had already opened the U.S. market to bitcoin perpetual futures that month. Rivals have moved into the same space. Kraken launched CF

item.title: NASA Conducts Latest RS-25 Engine Test in Support of Future Artemis Missions
item.description: 1 min read Preparations for Next Moonwalk Simulations Underway (and Underwater) NASA conducts a hot fire test of RS-25 engine No. 10001 on the Fred Haise Test Stand at NASA’s Stennis Space Center near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, on Nov. 18, 2026. NASA/Danny Nowlin NASA conducts a hot fire test of RS-25 engine No. 10001 on the Fred Haise Test Stand at NASA’s Stennis Space Center near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, on Nov. 18, 2026. NASA/Danny Nowlin NASA conducts a hot fire test of RS-25 engine No. 10001 on the Fred Haise Test Stand at NASA’s Stennis Space Center near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, on Nov. 18, 2026. NASA/Danny Nowlin NASA tested RS-25 engine No. 10001 on Nov. 18 on the Fred Haise Test Stand at NASA’s Stennis Space Center near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi. Test teams fired the developmental engine for the planned duration of three minutes and 20 seconds (200 seconds). While this developmental engine will not be used in flight, the hot fire test provides NASA and NASA’s prime contractor L3Harris Technologies with the capability to capture critical data to improve engine performance and reliability for future Artemis missions. For the Artemis IV Moon landing mission in 2028, the SLS rocket will launch astronauts aboard the Orion spacecraft from NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida. This mission will be a key step in the agency’s broader goals to explore the lunar South Pole, establish an enduring human presence on the lunar surface, and build on the agency’s foundation for the first crewed mission to Mars. For each Artemis mission, four RS-25 engines produce up to 2 million pounds of combined thrust to help launch the SLS rocket. All RS-25 engines are tested and proven flightworthy at NASA Stennis prior to use. Tests are conducted by a team of operators from NASA, L3Harris, and Nova Space Solutions. Learn more about Artemis

item.title: NASA’s Voyager 1 Makes History Reaching One Light-Day From Earth
item.description: Voyager 1, depicted in this artist’s concept, reached one light-day from Earth on Nov. 18, 2026. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech NASA’s Voyager 1 probe, humanity’s farthest-flying spacecraft, has reached one light-day from Earth, after more than 49 years of constant travel. A light-day is the distance light travels in 24 hours, equaling about 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers). The spacecraft achieved the milestone at 2:16 a.m. PST (5:16 a.m. EST) Nov. 18. Voyager team members at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California, managed by Caltech, heard from the probe 24 hours later, the time it took for the spacecraft’s radio signal traveling at the speed of light to reach Earth, early Thursday. “Traveling a light-day is a singular feat for a spacecraft, but Voyager is so much more than a distant traveler. The Voyager mission would be remarkable just for what it contributed to planetary science with the Grand Tour of the outer planets,” said Joe Westlake, director, Heliophysics Division at NASA Headquarters in Washington. “But it went on to become central to NASA’s fleet of heliophysics missions offering insights into the star that we all revolve around, the Sun.” Scientists use light to measure the vast distances of space. Light travels at about 186,000 miles (299,000 kilometers) a second in a vacuum. A ray of sunlight passing Earth takes about 1.3 seconds to reach the Moon, about four hours to reach Neptune, and another 20 hours to reach Voyager 1. For comparison, a light-year is 5.88 trillion miles (9.46 trillion kilometers). Even though the team has not received science and engineering data from Voyager 1 since Nov. 14, the spacecraft is sending what is called a carrier signal, which typically conveys that data to Earth. Mission engineers used the carrier signal and trajectory calculations to confirm the light-day milestone. They continue to analyze the issue impacting the science and engineering data. Humanity’s only probes in interstellar space, Voyager 1 and its twin, Voyager 2, launched in 1977 to take advantage of a rare planetary alignment. Managed by JPL, they were only the third and fourth spacecraft to visit Jupiter and Saturn, and the first to return high-resolution imagery, transforming our understanding of these worlds and their moons. Voyager 2 went on to study the ethereal ice giants, Neptune and Uranus. Both spacecraft continue to measure changes in the Sun’s magnetic field across vast distances. “Voyager 1 crossing the light-day threshold is yet another historic feat on an extraordinary voyage of discovery,” said Dave Gallagher, JPL director. “Above all, this milestone stands as a testament to the exceptional teams who built, programmed, and fly these spacecraft today, and who have overcome countless challenges to keep them connected to Earth across the vastness of space. As NASA pushes toward new frontiers in human and robotic exploration, Voyager and the people behind its success continue to inspire us to reach f

item.title: Russia’s Central Bank to Let Retail Investors Trade Bitcoin on Margin
item.description: Bitcoin Magazine Russia’s Central Bank to Let Retail Investors Trade Bitcoin on Margin Russia’s central bank plans to let ordinary investors trade bitcoin and other crypto on margin, capped at 300,000 rubles with a broker, a senior Bank of Russia official said this week, days after retail buying became legal. Olga Shishlyannikova, director of the central bank’s department of investment financial intermediaries, outlined the plan at the Ural Conference hosted by NAUFOR, the national association of securities market participants, RBC Investments reported. She said the margin rule and two other acts are under review at Russia’s Justice Ministry, and the regulator expects them to be registered by the end of 2026. It is not yet clear whether the 300,000-ruble margin limit for non-qualified investors will be shared with the existing cap on crypto purchases or counted separately. The central bank first published draft margin rules in July. Under that draft, brokers could accept cryptocurrencies as collateral for margin positions, and their clients could sell short. Both qualified and non-qualified investors would be able to trade on margin, with retail crypto trades subject to limits set by the Bank of Russia. The draft also added crypto to the risk-coverage ratios brokers use to police leveraged trades. Those ratios set how far a broker can lend against a client’s portfolio and when positions are forcibly closed. Crypto funds expected in 2027 Shishlyannikova also said the central bank expects the first Russian mutual funds that hold crypto directly to appear in 2027. Professional market participants have already filed applications to register such funds, she said. “Yes, we are considering the possibility next year of amending the relevant regulations to allow funds intended for qualified investors to buy cryptocurrency,” Shishlyannikova said. The regulator is not considering the same access for funds sold to non-qualified investors, she added. In late September, the central bank allowed fund managers to invest qualified investors’ money in cash-settled instruments tied to crypto prices, in a directive registered with the Justice Ministry. The proposed change would let those funds hold the coins themselves. Futures for retail can wait Retail access to crypto futures will take longer. Deputy Governor Philipp Gabunia told reporters on Thursday that the Bank of Russia could let non-qualified investors trade crypto-linked futures once the spot market is running, if it sees no risks, Interfax reported. “For non-qualified investors, this could be a very sensitive story. Let’s launch, and now we’ll see how it starts to work,” Gabunia said. “If we don’t see risks, we’ll allow it. Non-qualified investors will have to be a little patient.” Gabunia said the market’s shape could still shift, including which coins are admitted and which derivatives are offered on them. “Legislation is now changing this configuration a lot,” he said. item.title: ICJ rules Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya
item.description: In August 2017, after attacks by a Rohingya militia, Myanmar’s army launched a “clearance campaign” in Rakhine state, with survivors describing mass killings, rapes and burned villages as hundreds of thousands fled to Bangladesh. The Gambia took Myanmar to the ICJ in 2019, and after a seven-year legal fight the court has ruled that Myanmar committed acts of genocide. Meanwhile some 1.2 million Rohingya remain in crowded camps, unable to return home.

item.title: Mouse fight club might explain why we like to watch violent things
item.description: Credit: J.M. Iravedra-Garcia et al., 2026 Credit: J.M. Iravedra-Garcia et al., 2026 There's something about watching violent events that broadly appeals to us, whether it's the latest John Wick movie, a video game, or a live UFC bout. Scientists have debated whether watching violent things could make us more aggressive, but it could also be an adaptive survival strategy. Male mice, for instance, who watched other mice fighting learned enough about how to fight to better protect themselves (compared to mice who didn't watch fights) when pitted against stronger, more aggressive opponents, according to a paper published in the journal Nature. The team randomly assigned male mice to three groups—fighters, spectators, or novices—and then subjected each group to eight days of training with three 10-minute sessions per day. The novices played with stuffed mice in isolation, while the spectators watched various pairs of fighter mice battle from a raised platform behind a transparent barrier—a set-up chosen to let them smell and listen to the fights as well as observe them. The ninth day was "fight night," when all the mice had to face a daunting opponent in three 4-minute rounds. Each fight was filmed from above so that the mouse behavior could be analyzed. To monitor corresponding changes in brain activity, the team engineered the rodents' excitatory brain cells to glow green whenever they were activated, while inhibitory brain cells glowed red. They also implanted tiny optical fibers into 12 interconnected brain regions so they could track changing activity in every brain region simultaneously. Read full article Comments

item.title: Qualcomm offers test drive of its rack-scale Nvidia AI challenger
item.description: Qualcomm has opened cloud-based trials of its Dragonfly AI200 rack-scale inference system to selected customers through Cirrascale Cloud Services. Dragonfly AI200 is Qualcomm's pitch for running large language, multimodal, and other AI models without Nvidia-sized power and operating bills. Whether it delivers those savings is something customers can now put to the test on Cirrascale's AI Innovation Cloud, with a route into production deployments, Qualcomm says. Cirrascale also demonstrated the system at SC26 in Chicago on November 17-18. The AI200 is part of Qualcomm's Dragonfly datacenter lineup, which also includes the AI250 and AI300 accelerators and the C1000 server CPU. The company set out its broader ambitions at its Investor Day in June . Each AI200 accelerator card carries 768 GB of LPDDR memory, with 56 cards providing about 43 TB in a liquid-cooled rack. Qualcomm says the system supports models ranging from 7 billion to 10 trillion parameters, including long-context, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and agentic workloads. As we previously explored , packing in memory doesn't necessarily mean matching Nvidia's performance. Its Blackwell-based NVL72 systems use fast – and costly – HBM3e stacks, while Qualcomm has opted for LPDDR, more commonly found in mobile devices. "AI inference is becoming one of the largest and most important computing workloads in the datacenter, and the industry needs a more efficient approach," said Tony Pialis, Qualcomm's executive vice president and general manager for datacenter. He claimed that the AI200 brings the company's experience with high-performance, low-power computing to a rack-scale infrastructure, in an architecture designed around the performance, memory, and cost requirements of inference workloads. "Our customers need efficient, scalable infrastructure that can support increasingly sophisticated models without allowing power and operating costs to become the limiting factor," said Cirrascale CEO Dave Driggers. "By working with Qualcomm, we can give customers evaluation access to a compelling new architecture purpose-built for the next generation of AI inference." The chip firm also has its own software stack, the Dragonfly AI Infrastructure Management Suite, for provisioning, monitoring, workload orchestration, and fault handling across rack-scale deployments. ®

item.title: Bitcoin Price Rebounds Near $64,000 as Anthropic IPO Lifts Tech Stocks
item.description: Bitcoin Magazine Bitcoin Price Rebounds Near $64,000 as Anthropic IPO Lifts Tech Stocks The bitcoin price climbed back to near $63,700 on Thursday morning, according to Bitcoin Magazine Pro data, as Anthropic’s record initial public offering lifted tech stocks and stock futures ahead of the U.S. open. Bitcoin dipped near $62,000 late Wednesday after Federal Reserve minutes pointed to more rate hikes. It recovered overnight and briefly touched about $64,000 around 6 a.m. ET before easing slightly. The bitcoin price remains down roughly 11% from a week ago, when it traded above $71,000, and more than 20% below the roughly $82,200 level of a month ago. Anthropic IPO lifts risk appetite Anthropic priced its IPO at $83 per share on Wednesday, above its $70 to $78 range. The company sold about 980 million shares and raised $81.3 billion, topping SpaceX’s record offering in June, CNBC reported . The stock is set to begin trading on the Nasdaq on Thursday under the ticker ANT, with a fully diluted value of about $1.5 trillion. The pricing sent Nasdaq-100 futures up 2% early Thursday, while S&P 500 futures added 1.1% and Dow futures rose about 299 points. Chipmakers led the move, with Nvidia (NVDA) up 1.5% and Micron Technology (MU) up almost 5% in premarket trading. Some analysts had argued that investors were selling bitcoin to raise cash for the deal. Others questioned how much that selling actually weighed on the bitcoin price. With pricing now done, the bounce in crypto has tracked the broader rebound in tech. Gray market trading pointed to Anthropic shares opening as much as 24% above the IPO price. Crypto stocks rebound before the open Strategy (MSTR) traded near $93.90 before the bell, up about 4% after closing Wednesday at $90.32, down 6.4%. The company’s shares have fallen sharply alongside the bitcoin price this month, and a New York state pension fund boosted its Strategy stake by more than 10% in the third quarter, a 13F filing showed. Coinbase (COIN) rose about 3% in premarket trading to near $114 after a nearly 4% drop on Wednesday. Bitcoin miners also moved higher. Riot Platforms (RIOT) gained about 6%, extending Wednesday’s 7% rally, while MARA Holdings (MARA) and IREN (IREN) each climbed about 4% to 5%. ETF outflows and Fed risk weigh on the bitcoin price Demand from U.S. spot bitcoin ETFs remains weak. The funds shed a net $306.5 million on Wednesday, led by $148.7 million out of BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) and $69.3 million from Fidelity’s FBTC. item.title: Leonid meteor shower thrills stargazers worldwide with colorful sky show (photos/video)
item.description: null The Leonid meteor shower put on quite the show this week, with bright, colorful meteors thrilling stargazers worldwide and we've got the photos to prove it. The annual meteor shower peaked overnight on Nov. 17-18, with photographers braving chilly temperatures, clouds and even fog in hopes of catching the perfect shot. And for some, their patience certainly paid off. Leonids occur when Earth passes through debris left behind by comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, which orbits the sun approximately every 33 years. As tiny pieces of comet debris enter Earth's atmosphere at speeds of up to 44 miles (71 kilometers) per second, they burn up, producing bright streaks of light. The meteor shower is also famous for producing some of the most spectacular meteor storms in history. In fact, this year marks the 60th anniversary of the great Leonid meteor storm of 1966, when observers reported an astonishing 40 meteors per second at the peak. To mark the occasion, we spoke to people who witnessed the extraordinary event first-hand and you can read their remarkable accounts in our special feature . But back to the present! Let's take a look at some of the best photographs and videos captured during this year's impressive display. Photographer Austin Rebello drove several hours to Nubble Lighthouse in York, Maine, to meet up with fellow astrophotographer Rob Wright and hopefully capture a Leonid or two. "I specifically drove a few hours up there for hopes of capturing exactly this, as the radiant of the Leonids rose behind the lighthouse," Rebello told Space.com in an email. Leonid meteor streaks over Nubble Lighthouse, York, Maine. (Image credit: Austin Rebello) "My friend and I were lucky enough to also see it with our eyes, and it was definitely a top 3 meteor for me, as it was even bright enough to briefly cast shadows." A close up view of a Leonid meteor. (Image credit: Austin Rebello) Rebello also revealed on X that the meteor left behind a vibrant blue trail that remained visible to the naked eye for more than 30 seconds. The meteor left a vibrant blue streak that was visible to the naked eye for more than 30 seconds. (Image credit: Austin Rebello) Fellow astrophotographer Rob Wright was also at Nubble Lighthouse that night, where he captured the lingering trail of a particularly bright meteor on camera for an incredible 12 minutes, according to a post on X. "Turns out the smoke from the bright meteor early this morning was visible on camera for TWELVE (12) MINUTES just lingering there," Wright wrote on X . Turns out the smoke from the bright meteor early this morning was visible on camera for TWELVE (12) MINUTES just lingering there. I was able to make a rough timelapse video to show this.--November 18, 2026York, Maine https://t.co/pm9htHcMm3 November 18, 2026 This phenomenon is known as a persistent meteor train and is created when a bright meteor leaves behind a trail of ionized gas that continues to glow long after the meteor itself has disappeared. item.title: Nonprofit Common Space will launch 1st 'humanitarian satellite' in 2027
item.description: null The first satellite in a constellation designed for humanitarian use will lift off next year, if all goes according to plan. The nonprofit Common Space plans to assemble a six-spacecraft constellation of Earth-observing satellites , whose high-resolution imagery will aid first responders, journalists, scientists and human-rights investigators around the world. That plan firmed up a bit today (Nov. 19), as Common Space announced the builder of the first of those satellites : Satellogic, an Argentine-U.S. geospatial intelligence company. There are more than 1,000 Earth-observing satellites circling our planet at the moment. But much of the data they gather is proprietary or too expensive to serve the common good, according to Common Space. The nonprofit wants to change that via its envisioned constellation, which it says will collect imagery specifically for humanitarian and public-interest purposes. Common Space plans to operate on a "club-good model," which will share infrastructure and costs across a large community, allowing extensive, low-cost access to high-quality imagery. Satellogic is now officially part of this picture. "With Satellogic as our spacecraft partner, we're moving from vision to orbit and putting high-resolution data into the hands of those who need it most," Common Space co-founder Rhiannan Price said in a statement today. "This isn't just another satellite. We're building infrastructure to serve people for years to come." The satellite is Satellogic's NewSat Mark V, which Common Space selected after a competitive request-for-proposal process. Satellites can help first responders deal with natural disasters. Here, one of Vantor's Earth-imaging satellites captures the destruction Hurricane Melissa caused to Black River, in southwest Jamaica, in November 2025. (Image credit: Vantor Technologies/CC BY 4.0) The NewSat Mark V is just 32 inches (82 centimeters) long and weighs 85 pounds (38.5 kilograms) here on Earth . But the microsatellite packs a great deal of capability into that small package. From low Earth orbit (LEO), it naturally resolves features on the ground as small as 27.5 inches (70 cm), which Satellogic's proprietary algorithms can boost to a "super resolution" of 19.7 inches (50 cm). The satellite is scheduled to launch in July 2027, on a rocket that has yet to be announced. Satellogic will handle the preparations for that launch and manage satellite operations, which are expected to last at least five years in LEO. The company has extensive experience with such work; it has flown 61 of its Earth-observing satellites to date, all of which deployed successfully. And Satellogic is aligned with Common Space philosophically, the company stressed. "Common Space shares our belief that persistent global intelligence shouldn't be reserved for a few. Humanitarian responders and journalists are often first on the ground and last to get access, yet they need frequent, high-resolution imagery to see what's really happenin

item.title: Voyager 1 celebrates one light-day with a nice lie-down
item.description: Voyager 1 marked its milestone of one light-day from Earth in time-honored fashion: by giving controllers the silent treatment. On November 14, the mission team noticed that the veteran spacecraft had stopped returning science and engineering data. A Deep Space Network antenna in Canberra, Australia, picked up its carrier signal, but no data. The carrier signal indicates that Voyager 1 can still keep its antenna pointed at Earth and operate its transmitting equipment. However, something could be amiss with the system responsible for collecting and collating data from the spacecraft. Something similar happened in 2023 . After a few months of troubleshooting, engineers managed to coax a response from the probe, and by June 2024, NASA was delighted to announce that the spacecraft was back in action. The problem was traced to a faulty computer chip, and engineers devised a software update to work around the defective hardware. That experience will stand the team in good stead this time around. There was also a brief interruption in communications with Voyager 1 in October, which could have been caused by the spacecraft dropping into safe mode after a thruster failover occurred. Engineers are investigating whether the two incidents are connected. The Voyagers have an impressive amount of fault protection built in, which has contributed to their extraordinary longevity. It will be half a century in 2027 since the spacecraft were launched, so glitches are understandable and likely. NASA expects to confirm on November 19 that Voyager 1 was still operating when it reached one light-day from Earth on November 18, using its carrier signal and trajectory calculations. The day's delay neatly illustrates a major headache for engineers: communication latency. It now takes more than 24 hours for commands to reach the spacecraft, and the same amount of time for a response to be received. Diagnosing the fault could therefore take weeks or longer. ®

item.title: Microsoft To Do will soon become Microsoft Done
item.description: Microsoft has slipped some bad news into this week's Ignite AI puffery: the To Do apps are retiring on June 30, 2027, ending a journey that began with its acquisition of Wunderlist more than a decade ago. The confirmation came in an announcement about unified tasks and plans for Copilot and Microsoft 365. Until now, there was To Do or Planner (in basic or premium guise). The idea is "a single system for tracking your work as an individual, as a team, and as an organization." To Do contributes features to that future, but its apps don't get to join it. The problem is that Planner doesn't do everything To Do does. Microsoft would like users to migrate to Planner but, by the company's own admission , there are plenty of gaps. No native Windows or Mac desktop apps are planned to replace To Do; file attachments aren't supported on tasks in the Planner private plan, and there's no equivalent to To Do list groups in Planner. "Equivalent To Do printing and email-list capabilities are not currently planned for the replacement experience," and so on. Existing To Do tasks and lists won't migrate to Planner either. They'll remain accessible through Planner until June 30, 2027, but that access ends with the apps. Microsoft says the date does not itself trigger deletion of the underlying data. Personal Microsoft account holders are left in an even worse state: Planner isn't available to them, including Microsoft 365 Personal and Family subscribers. Microsoft's advice is to choose another task-management app and prepare to export their data. Export instructions are still to come, and exporting won't necessarily produce something another app can import. Very much a case of "don't let the door hit you on the way out." Unifying tasks and plans is a good idea – the current situation does create confusion, as Microsoft acknowledged. However, taking an axe to To Do, which was developed to be a successor to Wunderlist ( acquired in 2015 for a figure between $100 million and $200 million, an early action under Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella), seems extreme. Microsoft calls the replacement "a unified platform for people and agents across Microsoft 365" and stated: "This unified platform makes accessing Planner through Copilot, Cowork and Autopilot easier." Some users responding to the announcement were unimpressed, with one declaring "What a mess," and another asking if To Do might be spun off into an open source project: "Not everything needs to be put into an AI/Copilot agent." Indeed, it doesn't. But a useful service that doesn't ram Copilot and AI integration down customers' throats at every opportunity? That would never do. The message for To Do users appears to be: Get with the Plan(ner) or just get out. ®

item.title: Cyberattack on service provider exposes payee data at 40 Irish credit unions
item.description: An attack on software provider Wellington IT exposed saved payee details held by around 40 Irish credit unions, prompting a minister to criticize the company's delay in notifying them. Robert Troy, Ireland's minister of state with responsibility for credit unions, said the breach happened in October but many affected institutions only learned of it in recent days. Troy told Irish broadcaster RTÉ that the breach occurred "sometime in October," and Wellington IT's delay in providing details to its credit union customers was "not acceptable." News of the issues affecting Irish credit unions broke on Tuesday, although the government said at the time it was only investigating a "possible cybersecurity incident" in the first instance, and did not name Wellington IT until Wednesday. Affected credit unions said attackers exploited a vulnerability in their provider's online banking platform between October 2 and 4. The flaw was closed on October 6. Troy said the affected credit unions were only informed for the first time in recent days. The exposed records concern payees saved in members' online banking accounts. Those records can also be linked to the members who created them. The information exposed varies between institutions and individual records, but disclosures list the following data types: Names on payee bank accounts and saved nicknames Business Identifier Codes (BICs) International Bank Account Numbers (IBANs) Sort codes Payment references Internal reference numbers that do not identify customers Payee addresses Credit unions including St. Canice's said online banking passwords, PINs, and login credentials were unaffected, and that the exposed payee details did not provide access to members' accounts or funds. St. Canice's warned members not to transfer money in response to anyone claiming it needed to be moved to safety because of the breach. The CEO of Belfast-based Wellington IT, Colin Mitchell, said in a statement that the company notified the affected organizations "as soon as we confirmed the potential risk to customer data." He said Wellington IT has engaged outside cybersecurity experts to help investigate the breach, and reported the matter to the relevant authorities. Mitchell added: "We are directly supporting our customers in their assessment of the potential impact on affected individuals and to help them meet any applicable regulatory obligations. "We recognize the importance of this matter to our customers and their members and are treating it with the utmost seriousness. We remain focused on completing a thorough investigation and communicating directly with our customers as the investigation progresses." Owned by Canadian company Vencora, Wellington IT has offices in Belfast and Dublin, and provides credit unions with software, mobile apps, private cloud infrastructure, and fully managed services. item.title: How to tell a cyberattack from a plain old outage
item.description: Over the past week, anyone could be forgiven for wondering whether a Diehard IV –style cyberwar had finally arrived in the US. Across just four consecutive business days, a mass Microsoft exchange outage broke IT services for thousands of companies , a Federal Aviation Administration tech screw-up grounded airplanes across the country, a software problem affecting JPMorgan Chase caused another round of disruption, a United Airlines system glitch delayed flights yet again, and an NSA classified network’s downtime left the agency’s staff sitting at home waiting to return to their office at Fort Meade. In the midst of a US war with Iran and rising fears of AI-enabled hacking , this still-unfolding comedy of IT errors colliding across American infrastructure felt to plenty of observers like more than a coincidence. Yet there’s still no evidence that any one of these clustered technological failures were related, much less caused by hackers. Their improbable, sequential timing left Americans anxiously doomscrolling for signs of foul play. But in cases like these, it’s the job of cybersecurity analysts (and reporters at WIRED) to determine—vibes aside—whether the latest tech outage was actually an accident or the result of a cyberattack. item.title: What's next for NASA interstellar Voyager 1 probe after passing 1 light-day from Earth?
item.description: null Voyager 1 has reached a historic milestone in space — it now takes a light-day to send a command to the spacecraft, meaning a full 24 hours for Earth to hail the distant spacecraft. Since Voyager 1 and its twin, Voyager 2 , launched on an initial tour through the outer solar system in 1977, their missions have been packed with science. Voyager 1 looked at Jupiter and Saturn from up close before veering for a flyby of Saturn's moon Titan and Saturn's rings, a pathway that brought it above the plane of the solar system in the early 1980s. Voyager 1's faster path out of the solar system brought it to one light-day in distance on Wednesday (Nov. 18), while Voyager 2 — which took a slightly slower track to see Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune — will reach a light-day of distance in 2035. So what's next for the two Voyager spacecraft as they reach further into interstellar space? Exploring afar Interstellar space, which is the area where the sun's constant stream of solar particles within the heliopause gives way to the physics of interstellar space, has been a valuable harvest for both Voyagers. Voyager 1 crossed interstellar space in August 2012 and continues to get data, while Voyager 2 has done the same since November 2018. "Current science is continuing our investigation on magnetic field strength and direction, plasma density, and energetic particle detection. What is important is to measure how these phenomena change as the spacecraft travels further away from the sun," Suzanne Dodd, project manager for the Voyager missions at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), told Space.com in an email. Added to that will be the Voyagers' examinations of plasma and magnetic fields nearby the spacecraft, and a focus on any "solar effects" such as shocks or pressure fronts, added JPL project scientist Linda Spilker in an email. "Key Voyager science going forward includes observing the extent to which our sun continues to affect interstellar space, all the way out to Voyager 1," Spilker continued. "Where does the sun's influence end and pristine interstellar space begin? Perhaps Voyager may last long enough to answer that question." The team also wants to watch the magnetic field around the spacecraft continue to change direction from the sun, to interstellar space, Spilker noted. That finding was not expected when the Voyagers launched, so scientists are curious to know more — as long as the spacecraft can last, that is. The locations of Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 beyond the boundary of our solar system. (Image credit: NASA, ESA, and Z. Levay (STScI)) Power management Each Voyager continues to lose 4 watts of power a year; their launch power was 470 watts in 1977, and the nuclear power source continues to dwindle, requiring harder choices as the missions approach their 50th years of operations. Instruments have had to be shut off, and both the spacecraft were directed to perform a "Big Bang" of power redistribution earlier this year to preserve as much

item.title: TfL takes Oyster photocard website offline after attackers compromise customer accounts
item.description: Transport for London (TfL) has copped to another cybersecurity breach, this time involving the account details of around 265,000 Oyster photocard customers. The capital's transport operator told The Register it first became aware something was amiss on November 16, when Oyster photocard customers started receiving emails asking them to create accounts they already had. The emails came from TfL's own systems, the transport body confirmed, but were generated as a result of the compromise. "We immediately took the TfL photocard website down while this was being investigated," said Shashi Verma, TfL's director of technology strategy and revenue. "The protection of personal information is a priority for us, and I apologize to our customers affected by this incident." TfL reckons its speedy response spared a considerable number of customers from having their details compromised. The transport operator says it has since contained the incident and contacted those potentially affected, though it is rather more forthcoming about what the hackers didn't get their hands on than what they did. TfL says no passwords, bank or payment card details, or customer journey information were compromised. It also believes the names and dates of birth of children with Zip Oyster cards were unaffected. Among those whose accounts may have been compromised are holders of Zip Oyster cards – issued to children as young as five – as well as students, apprentices, care leavers, veterans, and Londoners aged 60 and over. Despite the assurances about passwords, TfL says it will ask all photocard customers to change theirs, along with their security questions and answers. Those in the habit of recycling passwords across multiple websites are being advised to change them elsewhere, too. TfL says it has yet to find any evidence that the compromised data has been used and has notified the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO). The transport operator hasn't disclosed how the perpetrators got into its systems. Existing photocards will still let holders through the ticket barriers, though anyone needing to renew one or check their journey history will have to contact TfL's customer services team while the website is out of action . There's no word yet on when it'll be back. "We hope to restore the affected website services as quickly as possible," Verma said. TfL should be well versed in dealing with data breaches by now. In March, the transport operator told The Register it had notified more than 7 million customers following its September 2024 cyberattack. The hackers had accessed systems holding customers' names, email addresses, and home addresses, while around 5,000 customers were contacted as a priority because their bank account details may also have been compromised. Two teenagers were subsequently charged in connection with the attack, which authorities linked to the notorious Scattered Spider cybercrime crew. item.title: Esther Adeyanju: This International Men’s Day, Let’s Make Room for Men’s Vulnerability
item.description: “Men are not wired to show emotions.” A male friend once said to me during an argument. He was so convinced that I wondered whether a manual somewhere explained how men were manufactured. According to him, men were created to be strong, endure pain and keep their emotions to themselves. That was simply how they were made. “So, because you’re a man, you’re not supposed to feel hurt, fear or disappointment?” I disagreed. He insisted that showing emotions was not in a man’s nature. Who made that rule? Who decided that men could experience pain but must never be seen expressing it? At what point did being a man become synonymous with pretending that everything was fine? The conversation wilted, but it has stayed with me, perhaps because my friend wasn’t expressing an unusual opinion. He was repeating a stereotype many of us have heard all our lives: “Boys don’t cry.” “Be a man.” “Man up.” Three little expressions, and somewhere between being told to be strong and learning to say “I’m fine,” I wonder how many men have forgotten what it feels like to be heard. Frequent questions men are asked: “How far? Work nko?” “When are you getting married?” “Have you bought land?” “How is the family?” And the famous Nigerian question that can make an unemployed graduate dread family gatherings: “So, what are you doing now?” We often inquire about their achievements, responsibilities, and plans. These aspects are important, but how often do we ask about their fears? A father who leaves home before sunrise and returns exhausted, burdened by the weight of school fees, rent, and family expectations. A young graduate who has submitted countless job applications, yet still smiles politely when another relative inquires why he hasn’t found a job. A successful professional whose LinkedIn profile showcases numerous achievements, while his personal life tells a story that no one has thought to ask about. We admire their strength, we applaud their sacrifices, and we celebrate their accomplishments. But what about what they are going through? The person everyone leans on also needs somewhere to lean. Society has an interesting checklist for measuring a man’s success. A good job, a house, a car, a wife, children and financial stability. Preferably, all achieved before a certain age. But if a man struggles to achieve all these, is his life any less meaningful? Surely, a man’s worth cannot be reduced to his bank balance, job title or ability to convince everyone that he has everything under control. There must be room for men who are still becoming. item.title: Sticky note on monitor provided keys to the company’s kingdom
item.description: Welcome, once again, to PWNED, where we talk smack about organizations that have smacked themselves down by practicing poor security hygiene. This week's story involves everyone's favorite low-tech password manager: the sticky note. Our terrifying tale comes courtesy of Christian Espinosa, a certified penetration tester with over 30 years of experience and the CEO of Blue Goat Cyber , a security company. Espinosa shared an experience where critical credentials were right out in the open for any person in the office to see. During a walkthrough of a client's office, he noticed a password written on a sticky note that was taped to an employee's monitor. While writing down your password and placing it in a physically secure paper notebook might be ok, taping it to the computer is definitely not. "Before I get my fingers on any system, I first walk the physical area that the system is located in — attackers do that when they're looking at a target too," Espinosa explained. “Physical security vulnerabilities are neglected much more often than technical security vulnerabilities and firms invest in firewalls where a sticky note is placed 3 feet from the front door." Espinosa took a photo of the sticky note and immediately tried logging into that employee's account. Success. Then, he tried the very same password on the VPN, which apparently had been maintained by that employee. Once he connected to the VPN, Espinosa had full access to the company network and all of its shared drives. He opened a shared drive that this employee had access to and there was an HR folder with all kinds of personally identifiable information (PII) about employees, including home addresses, driver's licenses, and scanned W-4 forms. There were even spreadsheets that listed everyone's salaries. The employee account also had access to a document that contained a list of internal server names and the names of the people in charge of each server (great for phishing). Another document had instructions for how to log into the accounting server specifically. The accounting server was a particular treasure trove of client information. On that server, Espinosa found a folder with vendor banking information, invoices, and payment records. "At that point, a password I had read from a sticky note during a walk-through had taken me from one desk to information that could have been used for payroll fraud, identity theft, or vendor-payment fraud," Espinosa said. After getting access to all this information, the pen tester presented his findings to the client. They quickly disabled the rogue account and started reviewing VPN access logs to see who else might have gotten into the network. They then searched the office to see if anyone else was exposing a password on a sticky note. Finally, they tightened permissions on the HR and accounting shares so that only people who really needed access to that data could get in. The lessons here are pretty obvious. Don't expose your passwords and, perhaps

item.title: Otherworldly image of a porcelain crab wins ocean photography contest
item.description: Tammy Nicholas’s winning photograph, Porcelain Crab Feathered Feast Tammy Nicholas This exquisite photo of a porcelain crab catching plankton while half-hidden in an anemone was named the overall winner of The Nature Conservancy’s Oceania Photo Contest . The blue of the shadows gives the image an otherworldly feel. Despite the name and appearance, porcelain crabs aren’t crabs – the similarity is a result of convergent evolution. The photo of the small crustacean was taken on a coral reef off Gili Air Island in Indonesia by Tammy Nicholas. A shot of a drifter or pelagic crab clinging to a piece of kelp, shown below, won second prize in the wildlife category of the awards. While it looks large, this crab is, in fact, just a centimetre across. The photo was taken near the Poor Knights Islands of New Zealand by Crispin Middleton. Advertisement Crispin Middleton’s photograph, named Ocean Drifter Crispin Middleton A photograph of water lilies growing in the Cenote Carwash near Tulum, Mexico, shown below, took second place in the prize’s plants and fungi category. Cenotes are sinkholes linked to water-filled caves, and this one got its name because taxi drivers used to clean their cars there. Its Mayan name is Aktun Ha. Vanessa Torres Macho’s photograph, titled Pendants Vanessa Torres Macho Vanessa Torres Macho took this image. The Oceania contest is open only to residents of Australia, New Zealand, Papua New Guinea and the Solomon Islands, but the photographs can be taken anywhere. A shot of sardines pursued by diving Cape gannets, shown below, took second place in the water category of the awards. This photo, by Justin Tan, was taken off Port St Johns in South Africa during the sardine run, when billions of sardines migrate north along the coast, for reasons that are still not understood. item.title: Uncensored AI models are thriving on code hosting platforms
item.description: Uncensored large language models (ULLMs) capable of producing harmful content are readily available at popular model-hosting websites, calling into question AI industry commitments to safety. Researchers affiliated with University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign in the US and Nanyang Technological University in Singapore have analysed 22,096 ULLMs collected from five major LLM hosting platforms. As described in their paper , "Characterizing the Ecosystem of Open-Source Uncensored Large Language Models: Supply Chain, Governance, and Risks," authors Zilong Lin, Zichuan Li, Xiaojing Liao, and XiaoFeng Wang found that uncensored LLMs are easy to obtain from hosting platforms like US-based Hugging Face, Kaggle, and John Snow Labs, and China-based OpenCSG and ModelScope. What's more, these unrestrained models have been deployed through applications, GitHub projects, and model routing platforms like Open Router, and users of those apps or services may not be aware of the nature of the underlying LLM. "Uncensored LLMs generally refer to LLMs whose content filtering or refusal safeguards are absent, removed, or weakened, allowing them to respond to requests that aligned models may refuse," the paper explains. Zilong Lin, lead author and assistant professor of computer science at the University of Missouri-Kansas City, told The Register that open source LLM hosting platforms like Hugging Face play a similar role to code hosting services like GitHub, GitLab, and Codeberg in the open source community by enabling sharing, modification, and redistribution of code artifacts. "However, unlike traditional software, whose behavior can often be examined through source code analysis, the safety alignment of LLMs is difficult to assess directly from their model files," Lin explained. "Evaluating whether an LLM has adequate safety safeguards typically requires deploying the model and testing its responses to potentially harmful prompts, which involves substantial computational and financial costs." Lin said this makes the identification and assessment of LLM safety particularly challenging, particularly given the large number of models available. That's why he and his colleagues chose to study the space through publicly available model metadata. Even popular commercial LLMs that are purportedly "aligned" – to some standard not everyone accepts – may respond to prompts with content deemed harmful. The US Government Accountability Office just released a report that found Claude, Grok, ChatGPT, and Gemini can be coaxed to provide information that would help with the planning of a terror attack. To highlight the consequences of AI advice, the GAO points to news reports indicating that generative AI helped enable the creation of an explosive device in a January 2025 attack on a Las Vegas hotel and the planning of a February 2026 mass shooting in British Columbia, Canada. item.title: How La Roche-Posay Brought Skin Science to Over 500 Guests in Its First Living Lab Experience
item.description: La Roche-Posay concluded its first Living Lab experience in Nigeria, welcoming Nigerian stakeholders to its opening party and three-day programme, held from 4 to 6 November 2026 at Oasis by The Five Palm, Victoria Island, Lagos. Inspired by the original Living Lab concept in Paris, the experience brought the science, research and expertise behind skincare closer to Nigerian consumers and healthcare professionals. It marked the brand’s first Living Lab in the country, creating a platform for more accessible conversations around skin health, dermatological innovation and everyday skincare. The experience opened with an exclusive session for healthcare professionals and invited guests before welcoming members of the public over the following two days. Each day featured three expert-led sessions exploring the role of dermatology and scientific research in advancing skin health, the wider impact of skin conditions on everyday life, and the importance of understanding product safety, tolerance and efficacy. The sessions brought together healthcare professionals and representatives from across Nigeria’s dermatological beauty and skincare community, encouraging knowledge-sharing and stronger connections between science, expertise and consumer education. Visitors explored five dedicated Innovation Corners showcasing La Roche-Posay’s Effaclar, Mela B3, Anthelios, Cicaplast and Lipikar ranges. Each space introduced visitors to specific skin concerns and the science behind the brand’s product formulations. Through interactive demonstrations and guided product experiences, guests gained a better understanding of different skin concerns and the role of targeted skincare in addressing them. At the Anthelios corner, visitors used a UV camera to see the effects of ultraviolet exposure and better understand the importance of sun protection. The Effaclar and Mela B3 spaces explored concerns including blemishes and hyperpigmentation, while the Cicaplast and Lipikar corners introduced visitors to approaches to caring for sensitive, damaged and dry skin. Beyond the Innovation Corners, visitors explored the Blue House, which presented La Roche-Posay’s history and commitment to dermatological innovation, and the Scars of Life Cinema. The cinema screened a 25-minute film exploring the physical and psychological realities of living with scars and scarring, including their impact on self-image and everyday life. The film also highlighted how Lipikar supports the care of skin affected by scarring, bringing attention to the importance of addressing both the visible and less visible experiences associated with skin conditions. The programme also created opportunities for visitors to engage with skincare experts and dermatologists through one-on-one consultations, ask questions about their individual skin concerns and receive guidance on building appropriate skincare routines. item.title: Google continues model chemistry experiment with Neon
item.description: Google periodically tables new AI models named after elements, and its latest offering has the noble name "Neon." "Engineered for long-running agent workflows, Neon sustains performance through complex, tool-heavy tasks end-to-end — whether running standalone or acting as a fast, high-judgment Orchestrator directing parallel Hydrogen subagents in Google Antigravity," explained Koray Kavukcuoglu, SVP at Google DeepMind and chief AI architect at Google, in a blog post . Neon emerged after Google last week emitted Hydrogen , after delivering Carbon two weeks earlier and wafting Argon out the door in late September. Unlike OpenAI's celestial more intuitive model naming scheme – Astra, Sol, Luna, and Terra – which maps celestial position to capability, Google's chemical soup doesn't suggest a specific hierarchy. To judge by price , Carbon or Argon would be Google's top tier model, based on non-discounted price that takes effect next month, each priced at $4/M input tokens, $20/M output. The Chocolate Factory refers to Carbon as "Our most capable reasoning model" while Argon is "Our efficient Gemini 4 frontier reasoning model … with faster responses and lower token spend per turn compared to Gemini 4 Carbon across complex coding, agentic, math, and science tasks." Yet Neon, the latest element in the mix, surpasses both in Artificial Analysis' Intelligence Index , scoring 61 compared to Carbon at 60, Hydrogen at 54, and Argon at 50. At the same time, Neon costs less, at $3/M input tokens and $15/M output. That favorable pricing is all the more surprising in light of Google's willingness, as of two days ago , to let users of its Gemini services opt out of generative AI model training without losing their chat histories. Kavukcuoglu evidently recognizes the need to clarify its model rankings, an issue addressed in a blog post section titled "Where Neon sits in the Gemini 4 family." "While Carbon tackles your hardest, long-horizon projects and Hydrogen handles fast everyday execution, Neon balances depth and efficiency," he explains. "Neon delivers frontier-level reasoning for complex, high-frequency workflows faster and more cost efficiently." That may not really clarify which model is appropriate for which task and frankly Google is fine with that. As noted, Google Antigravity comes with an Orchestrator that decides how to spend your money for you by swapping models on the fly. As the company describes it, a developer might start a task using Carbon, which would write a plan, and hand the task off to Hydrogen to benefit from its token thrift. Antigravity does support model pinning , for those who know what they want. But Google, like other companies exploring model routing and orchestration, is fine with developers delegating decisions that affect billing to their trustworthy service provider. ®

item.title: International Men’s Day: Six Films That Explore the Vulnerable Side of Men
item.description: One of the best aspects of art is its ability to imitate current events or imagine possibilities. Movies, as a powerful art form, present a sequence of events that allows viewers to see reflections of themselves or envision who they could become. At its core, art exists to entertain, inform and critique society. Through films, music and visual expressions, we are continually reminded of our shared humanity—our joys, flaws and contradictions. One subject that art, particularly film, has explored is masculinity. However, this theme is often addressed subtly and can be easy to overlook, as the movies that dominate global box offices frequently focus on spectacle: fantasy, romance, adventure or others. Conversations about men, their inner lives, vulnerabilities and social roles are often not in the top circle. Nonetheless, some films have attempted to explore what it means to be a man in today’s world. They invite audiences to contemplate important questions such as: What is the role of men in society? What defines a man? How does a man’s behaviour influence those around him? What expectations does society place on men? What responsibilities do men have within society? Where does responsibility begin, and where does it end? Do men matter? Do their feelings matter? The theme for this year’s International Men’s Day is “The Future Is For Everyone.” For that, here are some movies that explore and illuminate the complexities of masculinity: The Pursuit of Happyness This classic film reveals the vulnerability often hidden behind male perseverance. Will Smith ’s portrayal of Chris Gardner challenges the stoic notion of manhood by showing fatherhood as both an act of love and endurance. Through his struggles with homelessness, rejection, and exhaustion, the film redefines masculinity, depicting it as the courage to remain tender even when life tests your strength in every way. Fatherhood Kevin Hart ’s film Fatherhood delves into themes of grief and single parenthood, balancing humour with heartfelt moments. It challenges traditional expectations of masculinity by illustrating a father’s journey through uncertainty, learning empathy, and committing to being present for his child/ren. Through this film, Kevin Hart shares his vision of what it means to be a man and a father. Adolescence Adolescence examines how boys internalise distorted notions of strength and freedom, and how escaping them demands emotional awareness. The film reveals the journey of a young boy on the brink of adulthood, revealing the pressures of identity and self-definition. There is a lot to unpack from Stephen Graham’ s Adolescence about what it means to be a father and a child. King Richard A faction. In the narrative, King Richard shares the stories of Serena and Venus Williams , highlighting discipline and belief as fundamental expressions of a father’s love. item.title: GTA VI didn't break the internet, thanks to 'stupid DNS tricks'
item.description: Grand Theft Auto VI may put a dent in global productivity today but the game didn’t break the internet. For those unfamiliar, GTA VI is the first new instalment of the mega-hit game in 13 years and it is nearly impossible to understate the excitement surrounding its release. Anecdotal evidence suggests fans of the game may today report they suddenly feel unfit to perform paid work. Developer Rockstar Games allowed Xbox and PlayStation owners to pay for and download the 200GB-plus game on November 10, before play commenced on the 19 th . Millions took advantage of the chance to download the game, creating just the sort of internet traffic event that regional internet registry the Réseaux IP Européens Network Coordination Centre (RIPE NCC) can observe with its RIPE Atlas internet measurement network. RIPE data scientist Emile Aben, with help from staffers Alun Davies and James Cowie, went looking for GTA-related traffic and found some interesting patterns . Aben observed that traffic to PlayStations mostly came from content delivery networks operated by AWS and Fastly. Microsoft relied on Fastly for over half of traffic flowing to Xboxes and used Akamai too, but eschewed AWS's CloudFront. The data scientist observed heavy use of “GeoDNS,” a technique that returns different IP addresses for a single domain request, depending on a user’s location. DNS’s designers didn’t intend that. Indeed, the RIPE trio point out that Paul Vixie, the computer scientist who earned his place in the Internet Hall of Fame for massive contributions to the DNS system, regarded things like GeoDNS as “stupid DNS tricks.” Whatever you think of GeoDNS, the RIPE researchers found that folks who were likely downloading GTA VI from Los Angeles, Tokyo, and Istanbul were each directed to different sites. Their probe of a network in Shanghai, China, found “a very distinct long lookup-chain with a hostname that is associated with the Alibaba Cloud in the end that maps to six different IP addresses.” “This hints at specialised treatment for some countries/regions,” Aben wrote. He also noted that Internet Exchange Points, the interconnect facilities that network operators use to exchange traffic and shorten paths, had to cope with record traffic during the download period – and seem to have handled the load. Aben thinks the GTA VI download program offers a useful lesson. “DNS helps steer each player towards a download server, while multiple CDNs share the work of delivering the files,” he wrote. “That distribution matters beyond gaming. On the open Internet, game downloads share routers and link capacity with all kinds of other traffic, including critical services.” “Keeping downloads local helps leave capacity on long-distance links free for other uses, making that enormous demand manageable.” ®

item.title: How aquanauts could help save Florida’s reefs
item.description: It sounds idyllic. Who wouldn’t want to occupy a newly built residence in the Florida Keys, complete with its own coral garden right outside the window? The only complication is that it is 17 metres below the surface of the Atlantic Ocean. That is not putting off Jim Brittsan, though. “This is really exciting,” he says. Brittsan is the founder and executive director of coral restoration non-profit Sustainable Ocean and Reefs (SOAR). He is also the diver who arranged the temporary coral nursery beside the residence, having brought the corals from a site where, 10 metres closer to the surface, they faced increasing environmental stress. Now, in reduced temperatures, they are starting to flourish, hosting their own marine life – visible day and night, in all its busyness, from the underwater residence known as Vanguard just 15 metres away. Vanguard was deployed at Tennessee Reef in June 2026 DEEP and Brendan Hall Vanguard is a long-stay underwater station for marine biologists. It was deployed in June 2026 at Tennessee Reef on the seafloor of the Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary, around 8 kilometres south of Long Key. Its coral nursery looks like a strange marine shrubbery: the coral fragments are arranged on anchored ropes that stand upright in the water. Once Vanguard is operational, a more permanent nursery will be established and the corals will eventually be planted on the seabed as part of ongoing restoration efforts, with their long-term survival assessed through monitoring. Advertisement Resident scientists will be able to monitor marine life around the clock DEEP, the international design and engineering organisation that built Vanguard, aims to make humans aquatic by establishing more subsea habitats like it. These will allow people to live underwater for extended periods to engage in scientific research and conservation. This opens up unprecedented opportunities to do research because there is no need for divers to bounce up and down to a research vessel on the surface. Those round trips eat into valuable work hours, because divers can spend only limited time at depth and must ascend slowly to avoid decompression sickness. “If we’re diving from a boat, we can do about 3 hours’ work a day at depth,” Brittsan says. “It’s much more efficient if we can just stay down there.” Corals moved to deeper, cooler water beside Vanguard are recovering in a temporary nursery DEEP There is plenty of work to do in the Florida Keys. Elkhorn (Acropora palmata) and staghorn (Acropora cervicornis) corals, which are vital reef-building species, are now considered functionally extinct in Florida. But it is not just in Florida waters that corals are struggling. Climate change, which brings elevated ocean temperatures, is a significant threat to corals around the world. In warmer waters, corals eject the algae that live in their tissues. This upends their mutually beneficial symbiosis in what is known as a bleaching event – without the algae and other symbi

item.title: El Niño Rains Paint the Atacama
item.description: Earth Observatory Science Earth Observatory El Niño Rains Paint the Atacama Earth Earth Observatory Image of the Day EO Explorer Topics All Topics Atmosphere Land Heat & Radiation Life on Earth Human Dimensions Natural Events Oceans Remote Sensing Technology Snow & Ice Water More Content Collections Global Maps World of Change Articles Earth Matters Blog Blue Marble: Next Generation EO Kids Mission: Biomes About About Us Subscribe 🛜 RSS Contact Us Search September 14 October 24 NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison September 14 October 24 NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison September 14 October 24 Curtain Toggle 2-Up Parts of the Atacama Desert in northern Chile, normally one of the driest places on Earth, turned red-purple, green, and white in austral spring 2026 following an unusually wet winter. The rain woke seeds lying dormant in the soil, setting off what scientists say may be the most extensive desierto florido , or “flowering desert,” of the satellite era. The rains came as El Niño was strengthening in the tropical Pacific. During an El Niño, the subtropical Pacific high that normally keeps the region dry weakens, while a blocking high tends to form in the South Pacific near the tip of South America. Together, these shifts push the Southern Hemisphere storm track equatorward. Beginning in mid-July, a series of storm fronts fed by an atmospheric river brought one of the heaviest July rain events in decades to a long stretch of Chile, from the Atacama region south to Los Lagos, according to Chile’s national weather service (Dirección Meteorológica de Chile). In August, back-to-back winter storms blanketed parts of the Atacama Desert in rare snow . The spring blooms that followed are visible in these satellite image pairs, which show the desert at different stages of flowering on September 14 (left) and on October 24 (right). The OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 8 acquired the September images, and the OLI on Landsat 9 acquired the October images. The pair above shows a part of the desert about 30 kilometers (20 miles) southwest of Copiapó, near the eastern sector of Desierto Florido National Park. The red-purple areas prominent in the October 24 scene are vast blooms of pata de guanaco, most likely Cistanthe longiscapa or another Cistanthe species, according to Roberto Chávez, a remote sensing scientist at Pontificia Universidad Católica de Valparaíso. Patches of red-purple Cistanthe are visible during a bloom in the Atacama Desert, shown in this photograph taken on October 24, 2026. Matías Pérez-Evens and Roberto O. Chávez/LabGRS-Instituto de Geografía- Pontificia Universidad Católica de Valparaíso. Chávez and colleagues photographed the Cistanthe blooms (above) in the area that same day. They were in the field to study the bloom with satellite data, drones, and digital cameras. The project aims to use these data to map how the bloom’s biodiversit

item.title: South Korea tries to out exam cheats with Extreme Emergency smartphone alert
item.description: At 08:30 on Thursday morning every powered-on mobile phone in South Korea blared out an Extreme Emergency Alert tone for 10.5 seconds – but the nation was at peace, with no major natural disasters occurring. The extreme emergency South Korea hoped to avoid was cheating in the annual College Scholastic Ability Test (CSAT), an exam that over half a million people sit in the hope of securing admission to their preferred university. This year, around a third of those applicants are repeating the test after their previous effort didn’t get them the result they wanted. CSAT involves five separate examinations staged in a single day. Participants can only bring pencils to the test. Smartphones or any sort of tech is strictly forbidden. Which is why Korean authorities used the national alert system on the day of CSAT, because if the 40dB tone sounded in an exam centre, it could indicate a student had deliberately or inadvertently tried to bring a smartphone – perhaps as an exam aide. Korean media report the 08:30 alert turned up nine phones. Authorities will send a second alert tone at an unspecified time later in the day to again smoke out any surreptitious smartphones. It’s not possible to opt out of the alerts, one reason a concerned netizen has used the Android issue tracker to suggest sending alerts to detect exam cheats could be an abuse of the emergency alert system that Google might want to do something about. South Korea sends a lot of emergency alerts, for matters such as helping to find missing persons or to warn of dangerous weather. It’s not uncommon to receive several in a single day. Authorities also gave advance notice of the CSAT alerts, which will not, therefore, cause panic on the streets of Seoul or Busan. CSAT day is, however, a serious occasion. Some businesses open late so test-takers can get to their exams without having to battle peak hour traffic. Those measures are arguably less disruptive than the widespread internet outages that some states in India impose on major exam days. An alleged leak of one Indian exam paper saw the nation’s tech regulator ban messaging service Telegram in the country and eventually sparked a youth protest movement that New Delhi tried to suppress with more deliberate internet outages. ®

item.title: Turmeric supplements offer little benefit for knee osteoarthritis
item.description: Turmeric capsules are touted as remedies for joint problems olga Yastremska/Alamy Turmeric supplements seem to have little to no effect on pain and mobility problems caused by knee osteoarthritis. That’s according to one of the most rigorous assessments of the evidence yet, which focused on four randomised controlled trials comparing the supplements to placebo pills. Osteoarthritis, which affects more than 500 million people worldwide , is caused by damage to cartilage that cushions the ends of bones, resulting in pain, stiffness and inflammation. Standard treatments include painkillers and anti-inflammatory drugs that can ease symptoms. “But many people see little or no benefit,” says Philip Conaghan at the University of Leeds, UK, who wasn’t involved in the latest review. Read more There are only a few anti-ageing supplements that actually work Turmeric supplements are often touted as an alternative therapy. They contain curcumin, a compound that gives turmeric its yellow colour and is thought to have anti-inflammatory properties. Yet such beliefs are often based on prior flawed studies , says Ivan Shirinsky at the Research Institute of Internal and Preventive Medicine in Novosibirsk, Russia. Advertisement Shirinsky and his colleagues analysed results from four randomised controlled trials, collectively involving more than 370 participants with knee osteoarthritis. Participants were randomly assigned to take either a supplement containing turmeric extract or placebo pills two or three times per day, for between eight weeks and three months. Each trial used a slightly different supplement containing a different curcumin dose. “We looked at the most rigorous evidence available,” says Shirinsky. Among those who took a placebo, knee pain decreased by 1.6 points, on average, on a scale from 0 to 10 by the end of the study. Those taking turmeric supplements experienced an average 2.3-point decrease in pain, meaning the difference between the turmeric and placebo groups was half that required to be meaningful to patients based on prior studies , says Shirinsky. Free newsletter Sign up to Health Check Sign up to newsletter In line with this, surveys revealed that turmeric supplements had no meaningful effect on participants’ quality of life or their ability to carry out everyday activities such as walking, getting up from a chair or climbing stairs. “If somebody is taking one of these therapies and thinks it is helping their symptoms, I would never force them to stop,” says Conaghan, since it could be working for some people. “But the evidence suggests it’s not going to help you. I would save your money.” However, the findings cannot provide a definitive answer, says Shirinsky. “All included studies used different formulations of turmeric, and this reduced the certainty of the evidence,” he says. What’s more, the evidence wasn’t strong enough to make conclusions around turmeric’s potential side effects; curcumin supplements have previously been found t

item.title: Chinese web giant Tencent says new US GPU ban ‘sets everyone back in China’
item.description: The USA’s new ban on Chinese companies remotely accessing GPUs will have short-term impact, but ultimately see China accelerate its development of domestic alternatives, according to Martin Lau, the president of Chinese web giant Tencent. Speaking on the company’s Q3 earnings call, Lau said the new US regulation will have an “unfortunate” impact on Tencent’s business. “It does set everyone back. It sets everyone back in China,” Lau said. “So everyone is actually having less advanced compute to work with, no matter when you actually started leasing or building capacities outside of China.” He said the ban will impact Tencent’s ability to train models. “Our training efficiency with Hy4 is actually very high,” he said. “When we look at the next version, it would take probably longer time for us to come up with the next version in the short run.” “But over time, the domestic supply chain would actually come on board.” Lau also thinks the bans won’t hamper Tencent’s ability to run inferencing workloads, because made-in-China chips “should be able to cover it.” “And over the longer run, we believe all Chinese players would actually have to rely on domestic supply chains and domestic chips, which we see the industry is progressing very fast,” he added. “With the latest restriction, we expect it to actually speed up even further, because all the development effort would actually have to be focused on speeding up the domestic supply chain.” Tencent needs GPUs, and lots of them, because the 10 million users of its agentic assistant WorkBuddy are collectively consuming over 100 trillion tokens per day. Lau thinks WorkBuddy is on track to becoming a hit product, partly because many users are outside China. Lau said Tencent can serve WorkBuddy customers outside China because the service can operate with different models, and the company thinks it can find third parties to provide the necessary inferencing services without the new US bans creating a problem. But Lau said that GPU rentals and other cloud services, which are also growing strongly, may be impacted. “In terms of cloud, if it is non-GPU related, we can actually build capacities ourselves outside of China,” he said. “I think there is still a lot of such opportunities because our cloud service is actually very cost competitive. When it comes to GPU, then unfortunately, we cannot actually offer high-end GPU anymore. We may be able to work with some partners in different places.” Tencent doesn’t break out revenue for its cloud services, but said they rose by 35 percent year-on-year, well ahead of the company’s overall eight percent growth. Marketing services also grew strongly, by 19 percent, thanks in part to new AI-powered systems that improve ad targeting. The company’s WeChat and Weixin messaging platforms continued to grow, adding 35 million accounts to exiting the quarter with 1.44 billion monthly active users. item.title: Ukraine blew up Putin’s bridge using relay drones to bypass Starlink limits
item.description: A Ukrainian barrage of missiles and drones collapsed a crucial segment of Russian President Vladimir Putin’s prized Kerch Strait Bridge—and Ukraine’s military pulled off the strike deep within Russian-occupied territory without relying on the military-grade version of Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite communications to guide the missiles in. On the nights of November 15 and November 16, coordinated waves of Ukrainian drones and missiles caused enough damage to collapse one of two steel arches supporting the Kerch bridge’s roadway for automobile traffic, according to an Institute for the Study of War update . Russian sources claimed several hundred Ukrainian drones first overwhelmed Russian air defenses to pave the way for remote-controlled missile strikes focused on the bridge, with the latter prominently including Ukraine’s homegrown Flamingo cruise missile. The Ukrainian operation adapted a Russian battlefield innovation by using drones equipped with mesh radios to create an airborne communications network, according to the Financial Times . Each networked drone acts as a relay node to extend the communication link between human operators and remotely piloted missiles and strike drones. Russia began using the technique to support long-range drone and missile strikes on Ukrainian cities. Read full article Comments
