item.title: Supernova explodes before astronomers' eyes | Space photo of the day for Nov. 18, 2026
item.description: null Before-and-after photos showing the appearance of a new supernova designated SN 2026ahvu. (Image credit: Dark Energy Survey/DOE/FNAL/DECam/CTIO/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA. http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/. Acknowledgment: PIs: G. Narayan & T. Murphey (University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign) Image processing: M. Zamani & D. de Martin (NSF NOIRLab)) A new supernova has been spotted exploding in the spiral galaxy NGC 1433, about 50 million light-years from Earth. What is it? Researchers have discovered a new supernova called SN 2026ahvu. A Type Ia supernova, this event took place in a system with two stars orbiting one another (also known as a binary system), in which typically one star is an exploding white dwarf . During most type Ia supernovae, the white dwarf pulls material away from the other star until enough accumulates on its surface to create an explosion. Finding galaxies where stellar explosions are taking place isn't a rarity. However, this supernova is unique in how early it was captured. If the supernova were starting to dim, researchers might infer that the event was ending. However, according to details shared when it was first spotted, as well as later observations, this supernova was discovered while getting brighter. This indicates that the supernova was likely caught early in the process of exploding, providing researchers with a unique opportunity to observe the event as it is taking place. By exploring observations of the galaxy before, during and (in the future) after the supernova event, researchers can investigate this type Ia supernova and how it affected the system in which it took place. Why is it incredible? Scientists made this discovery using ATLAS, or the Asteroid Terrestrial-impact System, which is a robotic astronomical survey made up of telescopes across both hemispheres. ATLAS is designed to spot incoming near-Earth objects like asteroids before they can reach Earth. It's essentially an asteroid impact early warning system. But just because that's what the system is designed for doesn't mean that's all it can do. The system can also spot other objects moving through space and, in this instance, it was able to capture observations of this supernova. Following its initial discovery, other observations of the supernova were made using NOIRLab's Dark Energy Camera (DECam) and Gemini South telescope.

item.title: AI-powered cyber threats are changing the rules of enterprise recovery
item.description: Cybersecurity has long been a contest between attackers finding new ways in and defenders trying to keep them out. Artificial intelligence is making that contest more complicated, giving cybercriminals new ways to develop and adapt their attacks while putting additional pressure on conventional cyber defences. For enterprise IT leaders, the challenge extends beyond preventing a breach. What happens when an attacker gets through? Can compromised data be identified, clean copies recovered, and essential systems brought back online without prolonged disruption? These questions are becoming increasingly important as organizations confront both traditional threats and emerging AI-powered cyberattacks. A successful defense strategy must, therefore, account for what happens after an incident, not just the measures designed to prevent one. Making recovery part of the defence This is where cyber-resilient enterprise storage has an important role to play. Rather than relying solely on traditional backup processes, organizations need ways to protect critical data, detect potential compromise, establish which copies can safely be recovered, and restore those copies as quickly as possible. Infinidat addresses this challenge through its InfiniBox and InfiniBox SSA enterprise storage platforms, which incorporate the company’s InfiniSafe cyber resilience and recovery software suite. InfiniSafe combines immutable snapshots, which cannot be altered or deleted during their protected retention period, with logical air-gapping to isolate the management plane from the data plane. Fenced forensic environments provide a separate space for validating data before recovery. The technology also supports automated cyber protection, allowing security monitoring data center wide cyber security software applications or a Security Operations Center (SOC) to automatically talk to InfiniBoxes and trigger immutable snapshots when suspicious activity is detected. This helps reduce the window in which critical data might be exposed. For organizations concerned about recovering compromised information, optional InfiniSafe Cyber Detection uses AI-based analysis to help identify cyber affected data and locate the last known good copy of the data for recovery. Speed is another consideration. Infinidat guarantees recovery of immutable snapshots in one minute or less for InfiniBox and InfiniBox SSA, subject to the guarantee’s terms and conditions. Ultimately, cyber resilience isn’t about assuming every cyberattack can be stopped. It’s about ensuring that when defences are breached, organizations have the tools and processes to recover trusted data and limit the operational consequences. For enterprise IT teams, that makes recovery readiness an essential part of the cybersecurity conversation. Sponsored by Infinidat

item.title: Space robot legend Voyager 1 is now more than 1 light-day away
item.description: NASA's Voyager 1 probe is now more than one light-day from Earth – so distant that a radio signal takes 24 hours to reach it. The veteran spacecraft has spent almost 50 years getting there. Voyager 1 was launched on September 5, 1977, from Cape Canaveral in Florida. Planning for the mission began in the 1960s, while NASA was working feverishly to put a man on the Moon ahead of the Soviet Union. A rare alignment of the outer planets made a tour of Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune possible. Voyager 2 eventually visited all four; Voyager 1's route prioritized Saturn's moon Titan, ruling out a subsequent encounter with Pluto. Voyager 1 completed a flyby of Jupiter in 1979, and passed Saturn and Titan in 1980. Its final imaging sequence in 1990 produced the solar system "Family Portrait," including the famous Pale Blue Dot image of Earth. The cameras were then switched off for good. Thirty-six years after those final pictures, Voyager 1 remains in contact with Earth, with two science instruments still operating: the magnetometer and plasma wave subsystem. Others have been shut down over the decades to conserve the dwindling power supplied by its radioisotope thermoelectric generators (RTGs). Dr Garry Hunt, a member of Voyager's original imaging team, told The Register : "Voyager's real success is the way it used reliable equipment. Well-tested Mariner equipment, and special new things that had come about for it. "We had fault protection on board as well. If anything goes wrong, it automatically switches to a backup. So there was always a backup. There was always a safe mode. We had to have radiation protection on board … when we designed this, we didn't really know the magnetic environment around Jupiter, and to be told it was so strong, 1,000 times stronger than we anticipated, really threw everything up in the air, and so that had to be dealt with." Hunt paid tribute to the succession of project managers and engineers who have kept the probe running over the years. "I think this was a really wonderful example of project management, of clever management of engineering, and interesting science coming out of it, which has made history books and gone to be a catalyst for other things in the future," he said. Voyager 1 may now take two days to answer a call from Earth. After almost 50 years, the remarkable thing is that it still answers at all. ®

item.title: StubHub International warns customer data may have left the venue
item.description: Ticket resale giant StubHub International has warned customers that a recent breach may have exposed their personal information to cybercriminals. The company said it detected "unauthorized access to certain systems" on its platform between late October and early November. Customer notification emails seen by The Register list potentially affected information including names, email addresses, phone numbers, and country or regional settings. StubHub International, operated by Ticketbis S.L., apologized for the intrusion and offered the usual promise to implement security enhancements after the fact. The company said it had addressed "certain vulnerabilities" while containing the incident and was continuing to monitor for suspicious activity. Outside cybersecurity experts are assisting with the ongoing investigation. The company warned that any exposed information could be used to make subsequent scams more convincing. "To date, we have found no evidence of unauthorised access to account passwords , banking information or payment card details," the email stated. "We also have no evidence that the compromised information has been used fraudulently. "However, there is a risk that third parties could use this information to attempt fraud, identity theft or phishing through emails, messages or calls that appear to come from StubHub International or other trusted organizations." The Register contacted StubHub International for more information, such as how many customers were affected, but it did not respond. Digital Fuel Capital bought StubHub International from Viagogo in 2021 after the UK's Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) required the international business to be sold to address competition concerns. In June, the CMA fined Ticketbis £889,200 and ordered refunds exceeding £590,000 after finding that mandatory fees were omitted from upfront ticket prices. StubHub International also recently faced criticism for allowing a single ticket tout to advertise £1 million worth of U2 tickets, despite its stated opposition to ticket-buying bots. ®

item.title: The Lego Star Trek bridge diorama set should be your gateway to finally watching the Original Series
item.description: null It's not quite a five-year mission, but as Star Trek celebrated its 60th anniversary in September of this year (we may have mentioned it once or twice), I decided it was high time I finally watched the original Star Trek . Before this year, I hadn't seen a single episode of "Star Trek: The Original Series", as it's now known. I'm a millennial; I grew up on "The Next Generation", "Deep Space Nine" and "Voyager". By comparison, the old series (TOS) always looked so… old and naff whenever I saw clips of it. But now I have seen the original series. Over the course of 2026, I've ploughed through all 79 episodes, spread across three seasons. And you know what? It's pretty damn good. Even with the shiny 2006 remasters, you'll have to prepare yourself for some bad special effects work, but the scripts are interesting, the sci-fi concepts are out there, and the acting — especially from Shatner and Nimoy — is top-notch. And just as I finally discovered a love for this classic sci-fi series, what should drop into my lap? Why it's the new Star Trek: U.S.S. Enterprise NCC-1701 Bridge diorama set from Lego. Now I have more on my wishlist to add to the Best lego space sets. Boldly building where no one has built before Building the Lego Star Trek: Bridge diorama. (Image credit: Future (Ian Stokes)) Let's start with the Band-Aid rip: this set is $200. I know; it stings, especially when Star Trek promised us a future where money doesn't exist. But at 1701 pieces (nice, I see what you did there), it's much better value from a bricks-per-dollar perspective than the X-Files set we checked out recently. Still, that's no small investment for a toy, even if it will make a lovely display piece when it's built. As the name suggests, you get a full Lego-ified recreation of the bridge of the USS Enterprise (NCC-1701, no A, B, C, or D). This includes Captain Kirk's chair, the helm positions ahead of him (manned by Chekov and Sulu), and all of the surrounding computer displays where you usually find Spock, Uhura and Scotty. There's even a viewscreen that can sit in front of the crew, displaying an adorable Klingon commander facing off against Kirk. The minifigure bridge crew of the U.S.S. Enterprise (L-R): Nurse Chapel, Chekov, Scotty, Spock, Kirk, McCoy, Uhura and Sulu. (Image credit: Future (Ian Stokes)) Star Trek: U.S.S. Enterprise NCC-1701 Bridge: $199.99 Board the legendary starship and meet the crew of the U.S.S. Enterprise NCC-1701 for an amazing building experience. Recreate the iconic bridge and transporter room that served as the backdrop for epic scenes from "Star Trek: The Original Series". item.title: Business as usual, but Huang ain't coming back, says Nvidia
item.description: Nvidia's board says it has no plans to bring Jensen Huang back as the GPU giant reports quarterly revenue more than double that of a year ago. The AI infrastructure leviathan had some reassuring to do after its leather-jacketed rockstar leader left under a cloud last week. Huang had been central to its rise as the dominant supplier of AI compute. Newly appointed board chair Harvey Jones ruled out an imminent comeback, saying: "The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO." Jones said the board was addressing the fallout and strengthening oversight, pointing to the creation of a committee to scrutinize the firm's security policies and export compliance. Nvidia has also retained the services of talent spotters Heidrick & Struggles to help find a new leader, according to Jones. Interim CEO and chief financial officer Colette Kress struck an upbeat tone on the company's Q3 earnings call. The results gave her plenty to work with : revenue rose 103 percent to $115.8 billion, while operating income climbed 115 percent to $77.5 billion. "We're addressing strong demand for compute across a diverse and expansive set of end customers, including hyperscalers, frontier labs, AI natives, enterprises, and governments," Kress said. She raised Nvidia's outlook for fiscal 2028, saying that the firm now expects revenue to grow approximately 75 percent year-on-year. Analysts immediately questioned this, asking what gave Kress the confidence to raise the outlook, given all the uncertainty surrounding the future direction of the company. Kress cited growing demand and additional supply as reasons for lifting the fiscal 2028 growth forecast from 70 to 75 percent. When asked about the financing deals that Nvidia provides for some of its customers, Kress appeared to hint that some things might change. "Our neoclouds have been so instrumental in terms of both supporting enterprises and supporting many of the different countries around the world, particularly on the sovereign perspective. And we continue to be working with them," she stated. But she added: "I think we would look at this and take a very strong look in terms of the types of companies that we would want to help in terms of the financing, as a lot of things have changed over this last quarter... but we do have some very, very strong existing customers that we will be continuing to work with." Kress also said that Nvidia's rack-scale Rubin platform had generated nearly $20 billion in revenue in its first quarter of production shipments. She said the firm expects the major frontier AI labs to account for approximately 15 percent of its Data Center revenue this year. Kress said that Nvidia is no longer shipping licensed products based on its Hopper silicon to China, as scrutiny grows over Beijing's access to advanced AI technology, and so its future guidance does not count on any Hopper revenue from there. item.title: Windows Server 2028 won't be compatible by default
item.description: Microsoft has pushed Windows Server 2028 into public preview, with an eye on beefed-up security, new infrastructure support, and the inevitable nod to AI. Neil Hinnant, a director on the Windows Server team, talked up the security tweaks. There's a hardened Server Core configuration by default and a new security baseline. "Trusted Launch extends protection to virtual machines," he wrote . "Confidential VM support begins a journey to support integrity-protected runtimes on supported CVM hardware." Server Core will therefore arrive locked down by default – good news for security, potentially less so for administrators whose existing configurations depend on more permissive settings. "For years, Windows Server shipped compatible by default," wrote Senior Product Manager Christina Curlette. "Making the server secure was up to you, usually by applying the Security Baseline or your own hardening scripts after setup." With Windows Server 2028 (and starting from Windows Server Insider Preview build 29706), Server Core will be installed hardened. "Hundreds of security settings are on from first boot," Curlette wrote. "Because the defaults are now locked down, some things that worked on Windows Server 2025 may not work on Windows Server 2028 without changes. This includes older protocols, legacy authentication, and some management tools and scripts." For a company obsessed with backward compatibility, this is quite the step. Welcome though the hardening is, administrators will need to test carefully: working on Windows Server 2025 won't guarantee a smooth ride in the brave new world. AI gets a role on both sides of the security fence: helping uncover vulnerabilities and giving Microsoft another reason to sell servers. Windows Server 2028 is being pitched for running models locally, with support for accelerators such as AMD's Instinct MI350P. Not every server is destined to babysit a model, however, and the storage changes may be more immediately useful to enterprise administrators. Windows Server 2028 will enable native NVMe storage by default, along with NVMe over TCP and RDMA. Booting from ReFS is also planned, adding another item to the storage upgrade list. Intune management for Windows Server has also entered preview. Azure Arc, with its cloud-native management workflows, is obviously still around, while Intune brings a more familiar management interface for administrators already using it for endpoints. Hinnant acknowledged that this was a "major release," and it looks like the security hardening alone will require a good deal of thought from administrators before organizations adopt the eventual production release. Esben Dochy, Principal Technical Evangelist for SecOps at Lansweeper, told The Register that Microsoft had indicated that the hardened security only applied to new installations. item.title: India's SatLeo Labs wants to build a 'thermometer for Earth' in space
item.description:
Sharmila Kuthunur is an independent space journalist based in Bengaluru, India. Her work has also appeared in Scientific American, Science, Astronomy and Live Science, among other publications. She holds a master's degree in journalism from Northeastern University in Boston. 

AHMEDABAD, India — As climate disasters grow more frequent and severe, a young Indian space-tech startup is betting it can help the world act sooner by reading Earth's temperature from orbit in near-real time. SatLeo Labs, based here in western India, is building what it calls a " thermometer for Earth " in space. It plans to achieve its roadmap to deliver frequent, near-real-time thermal data through Pyro, a planned constellation of 15 microsatellites that will circle the planet in low Earth orbit by early 2030, if all goes to plan. Equipped with thermal sensors and onboard artificial intelligence , the satellites will measure the heat radiating from Earth's surface at a resolution finer than 10 meters (33 feet), which is sharp enough to map heat variations down to street level, the company says. "It's going to be that precise," SatLeo Labs co-founder Urmil Bakhai told Space.com in a recent interview. That level of detail, he said, helps distinguish temperatures across a single city and pinpoint urban hot spots, allowing governments and policymakers to plan targeted interventions and more heat-resilient city designs. The company is also targeting agriculture, and for good reason: Research suggests that thermal data can directly reveal water stress on crops days before leaves wilt, discolor or show other visible damage, unlike visible-light satellite imagery. Other uses the company is eyeing include spotting forest fires early, tracking industrial emissions and, on the defense side, detecting sudden temperature spikes from missile launches . Down the road, the team also envisions hyper-local uses. Near the top of its list are live heat maps built into navigation apps that could help gig-economy workers in India. These folks, who often ride motorcycles, could use the data to pick cooler routes during heat waves, said Bakhai. "We are in space, but we're solving problems on Earth ," said Shravan Bhati, SatLeo's co-founder and CEO. First, however, the company has to prove that its homegrown hardware works in space. On Oct. 1, SatLeo launched its first technology demonstrator, TAPAS-1, aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket as part of the Transporter-18 rideshare mission. Short for "Thermal Access Platform for Analytics & Solutions," TAPAS-1 is India's first commercial thermal payload in orbit and the first of SatLeo's three planned test payloads meant to validate its technology. Once complete, the 15-satellite Pyro fleet will scan all of the world's land surface at least twice a day, Bakhai said. Successful deployment of that fleet would make SatLeo one of just a few private thermal-imaging operators across the world, such as SatVu in the U.K. and OroraTech in Germany. The

item.title: Police arrest 15 over £1.5M 'we'll recover your losses' scam targeting elderly
item.description: Fifteen people have been arrested over an alleged scam that squeezed more money from investment fraud victims by offering to help recover their losses. City of London Police searched 17 London addresses on November 11 and apprehended 14 men and one woman. All have since been released on bail. Investigators say the suspected fraudsters posed as regulators to persuade previous victims that compensation was available. Reports submitted through the UK's Report Fraud service helped investigators trace the compensation pitch to around 3,000 recipients since October 2025. Most victims were elderly, police said. The offers arrived by letter and email, promising redress for earlier investment losses. City of London Police said the victims were initially targeted by a range of investment scams related to art, carbon credits, land, whisky, wine, and pensions, and that some took place more than a decade prior to their re-victimization. Targets were directed to a company that demanded a holding fee before supposedly reclaiming their money. Police say those who paid were left further out of pocket. "Today's action sends a clear message to those who target vulnerable people for financial gain: you will be pursued and will face robust action," said Nik Adams, deputy commissioner at the City of London Police. "Behind every fraud report is a real person whose trust has been damaged, and in some cases, whose life savings have been stolen. We know the impact of these crimes can be devastating. "This case highlights the importance of reporting fraud through the Report Fraud service. Information provided by victims helped investigators link reports together, uncover the wider conspiracy, and identify those involved. It is a powerful reminder that every report counts and can play a vital role in bringing offenders to justice." The investigation also extends beyond London, with police identifying locations linked to the case in Kent and Hertfordshire. The searches resulted in officers seizing cash, drugs, and other high-value items, including a watch worth around £230,000, with the total haul valued at more than £2 million. Police put losses identified so far at £1.5 million and expect that figure to rise as the investigation continues. Knowing the details of an earlier scam doesn't make a caller trustworthy, police warned. That information can be used to sell victims a second fraud. Report Fraud has also highlighted substantial losses in other scams affecting older people. Fraudsters exploiting positions of trust stole a reported £93.8 million during 2025/26. People aged 70 and over lost more than £51 million, with relatives, friends, carers, and others entrusted with their finances among the perpetrators. Report Fraud received 3,812 reports in this category. "The impact of fraud extends far beyond financial loss, especially when it is carried out by those who are trusted by the victim," said Mark Evans, president at the Law Society of England and Wales. item.title: Voyager 1 at one light-day: Historian revisits Golden Record's forgotten details
item.description: In the one light-day that humanity's most distant object has now traveled from Earth, there has been enough time for details about its creation—and what it left behind—to be discovered again. Voyager 1, which left Earth in 1977 on an initial mission to fly by Jupiter and Saturn (as well as the latter's moon Titan), crossed into interstellar space in 2012. Like its twin (Voyager 2), Voyager 1 carries a "commemorative phonograph record," in part as a nod to the 100th anniversary of the recording medium and as a message from humanity to whoever (or whatever) encounters the spacecraft on its journey through outer space. About those forgotten bits, ask Glen Swanson . While researching the history of the Golden Record, he uncovered the discs' overlooked second set of operating directions and located the duplicates that were made and distributed almost five decades ago. Read full article Comments

item.title: ULA says Vulcan lacked the oomph to get Amazon satellites to orbit
item.description: United Launch Alliance (ULA) says poor booster performance appears to have doomed Sunday's Vulcan mission, which lost an Amazon Leo satellite payload on the rocket's return to flight. ULA's initial assessment points to trouble almost immediately. "Early indications are that just after liftoff the launch vehicle experienced low booster performance," it said. As a result, stage separation occurred at too low an altitude, and the rocket was not traveling fast enough for the payload to reach orbit. The second stage appeared to perform well, with its RL10 engines operating as planned, but that wasn't enough to make up for the shortfall, and the mission failed . ULA lost telemetry approximately ten minutes into flight. An investigation is underway, led by ULA and overseen by the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), which had to activate two Debris Response Areas where debris was falling. The agency directs aircraft to leave these areas, and others are prevented from entering. Late Wednesday afternoon GMT, ULA posted an update stating that it looks like it might be the fuel supply rather than the BE-4 engines that caused the underperformance of the booster. The company wrote: “Preliminary indications are that the low booster thrust was the result of inadequate fuel supply from the vehicle to the BE-4 engines, not from the performance of the engines." Previous flights had been blighted by problems with the solid rocket boosters , designed to give the rocket a kick at launch. Those issues prompted a stand-down while investigators examined the cause. This time, ULA said: "All indications are that the solid rocket booster performance was nominal, following nozzle improvements implemented for this launch." Attention therefore turns to Vulcan's liquid-fueled core stage, powered by two Blue Origin BE-4 engines, though that does not establish an engine fault. Fuel delivery or another first-stage system could also be responsible, and the investigation is ongoing. The BE-4 also powers Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket, which exploded on the launchpad during a ground test in May. In August, Blue Origin boss Dave Limp said that the issue originated at the main oxygen valve on one of the BE-4 engines. Modifications were made to deal with the problem. The upper stage's apparently normal performance may offer some reassurance to NASA, although the investigation remains at an early stage. The agency dropped the delayed Exploration Upper Stage earlier this year and is pursuing a stretched Centaur V alongside its existing interim cryogenic propulsion stage as options for Artemis IV. NASA is targeting Artemis IV for early 2028 and Artemis V for later that year. ULA said: "We truly understand the impact this has on our customers and are committed to returning to flight as safely and quickly as we can." The failure also dents ULA's otherwise impressive launch record. A predecessor of Vulcan, the Atlas V, has a 100 percent success record for payloads reaching orbit. Howeve

item.title: 1 light-day from Earth! NASA's Voyager 1 probe hits huge milestone in interstellar space
item.description: null NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft is now one light-day from Earth — so far away that it takes signals a full 24 hours to reach the probe. Voyager 1 launched on Sept. 5, 1977, just a couple of weeks after Voyager 2 lifted off. But Voyager 1 launched on a faster trajectory than its twin and has just become the first spacecraft to ever reach one light-day away, which is equivalent to about 16 billion miles (about 26 billion kilometers), or the distance that one light particle travels in 24 hours. The milestone — which Voyager 1 hit today (Nov. 18) at 5:16 a.m. EST (1016 GMT) — shows the incredible ingenuity, technical ability and creativity from the teams at NASA that continue to innovate to keep this mission going nearly five decades later. "The Earth and Voyager are exactly 24 hours apart at the speed of light," Voyager Project Scientist Linda Spilker told Space.com. "It's a very special moment where Voyager 1 is about 16.1 billion miles away, and we're celebrating that moment because it's the first human-made object to actually reach one light-day distance." All things Voyager The two Voyager spacecraft have been on one serious ride since launching in 1977. And each of these twin probes has taken a unique and historic journey through our solar system and beyond. On Voyager 1's trip through our cosmic neighborhood, for example, it made countless groundbreaking observations of planets and moons that we had never before seen up close (or at all). The probe discovered a ring around Jupiter as well as the planet's moons Thebe and Metis. It also found five new moons and a new ring around Saturn. "Voyager 1 flew past the Jupiter system and took images of Jupiter's moon Io, and it actually discovered that Io is volcanically active. So, images that were taken showed these volcanoes that were actively erupting, and we learned that Io is actually the most volcanically active body in our solar system, which is just amazing," Cynthia Phillips, a project scientist for NASA's Europa Clipper mission, told Space.com about one of Voyager 1's many discoveries. The Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 probes both flew past Jupiter in 1979, on their way out of the solar system. Represented here is Voyager 2's encounter with Jupiter. NASA/JPL A close-up of Jupiter's Great Red Spot as seen by one of NASA's Voyager spacecraft. NASA/JPL-Caltech Voyager 1 took photos of Jupiter and two of its satellites (Io, left, and Europa). The new study says that moons orbiting a gas giant planet greater than 8 Jupiter masses could help astronomers detect a rogue planet. NASA/JPL A mosaic of Jupiter by Voyager 1. JPL Jupiter and two of its moons — Io, to the left, and Europa — as seen by Voyager 1 on Feb. 13, 1979. JPL/NASA Voyager 1 image of Jupiter's volcanic moon Io, showing the active plume of a volcano called Loki. NASA/JPL/USGS "And then, as Voyager 1 continued out to the Saturn system, it actually discovered that Saturn's large moon Titan has a very thick atmosphere surrounding it," she adde

item.title: UK.gov JV gets £178M Home Office hosting deal. Without competition
item.description: The Home Office has awarded a contract worth £178 million to a public-private hosting services joint venture - without competition - to support critical national infrastructure. According to a notice published last week , Crown Hosting Data Centres (CHDC) won the seven-year contract to support "essential national infrastructure underpinning the Home Office's most critical systems, including border security, the Police National Computer (PNC), and core intelligence environments." CHDC is a joint venture between the Cabinet Office, which owns 25 percent, and Ark Data Centres Ltd, which owns the rest. It was set up in 2015 for the express purpose of providing hosting services for the government. The award was made through an existing framework agreement, set up in February 2022, awarded to CHDC without competition via a Voluntary Ex-Ante Transparency Notice . The service is set to support Critical National Infrastructure, although the notice does not reveal specific services requested. Mention of continued support for the Police National Computer may raise eyebrows. The Home Office is managing the transition of the aging legacy system to the Law Enforcement Data Service (LEDS) under the National Law Enforcement Data Program (NLEDP). A notice in December 2024 said that the Home Office was "focused on the development and adoption of LEDS products to replace existing PNC capability across all police forces and other non-policing PNC consumers, enabling the retirement by March 2026 (the point at which PNC support will expire)." The government had previously set a target of decommissioning the PNC in 2022. The Register has asked the Home Office to clarify why Crown Hosting support is necessary beyond this date. The PNC – which is based on mainframe technology dating from the 1970s – was at the center of a scandal in 2021 when a technology failure led to the loss of 413,000 records of evidence . The incident, which left then Prime Minister Boris Johnson floundering in Parliament, was the result of a scripting error in code designed to weed out records to be deleted from the PNC, a system running on a Fujitsu BS2000/OSD SE700-30 mainframe-based at a datacenter in Hendon, London. In 2022, the Cabinet Office awarded a contract worth up to £250 million to CHDC, also without outside competition. ®

item.title: Grand Theft Auto VI: The Ars Technica review
item.description: Just a minute ago, I was shooting my way out of a cocaine deal gone wrong, darting behind furniture for cover. Now I’m sitting on the floor of my home, working through the instructions to construct an Ikea-style coffee table with my partner. A tiny heart with a plus sign pops up, showing that our relationship is stronger for this quotidian domestic effort. This is the contrast at the heart of Grand Theft Auto VI , a game that seems to revel in both action movie bombast and the mundanities of everyday life for an up-and-coming young criminal couple. The reimagined and expanded Vice City is still the grand, crude, satirical criminal playground you’d expect after 25 years of 3D Grand Theft Auto games. And that world is as full, detailed, technically impressive, and polished as you would expect after this latest installment received a reported billion-dollar budget and roughly a decade of development work involving thousands of Rockstar staffers. item.title: SAP opens AI to on-prem customers, but cloud commitments could shut smaller firms out
item.description: SAP's commercial terms could put its latest AI tools out of reach for many customers, particularly smaller businesses running a single ERP system, the new chair of its German-speaking user group has warned. Thomas Henzler, appointed chair of DSAG last month, told The Register that Joule Studio 2.0 – SAP's upgraded platform for developing and deploying AI agents to automate business tasks – is a leap forward. Yet DSAG, which represents SAP users in Germany, Switzerland, and Austria, remains in talks with the vendor about the commercial conditions attached to access. In July 2023, CEO Christian Klein told investors that SAP's "newest innovations and capabilities" will only be delivered in the public or private cloud using RISE with SAP, the vendor's lift-shift-and-transform program launched with partners and cloud providers in early 2021. Customers running ERP software on-premises, or hosting it with a hyperscaler outside RISE, will miss out, he said. However, in May this year, SAP appeared to perform a U-turn . It said on-premises customers could access Joule 2.0 if they commit to a cloud "journey" through RISE with SAP, changing their support and commercial arrangements while migration projects are still underway. Henzler told The Reg : "There is a gap between the customer's reality and SAP's strategy for the autonomous enterprise. A lot of customers are still planning to migrate to S/4HANA, and now the question is, 'what do we have to do to use SAP AI, and what does it mean regarding the cloud strategy?' "Now it's a completely new strategy, a new approach, and a new underlying technology. The question is, what does it mean for existing projects, S/4HANA migrations, cloud migrations and so on? Is it necessary to rethink all the projects? Is there a big shift in the technology and architectures?" The DSAG chair said the biggest challenge in connecting legacy on-prem systems, such as ECC, to the new Joule suite is the commercial model. "Access requires a substantial RISE commitment and a minimum cloud-to-on-premise maintenance ratio. In practice, this creates a problem for customers with only one ECC system. To meet the cloud threshold, they have to convert their entire on-premises maintenance into a cloud subscription, which defeats the purpose of an on-premises connector. Consequently, the model only works for large enterprises with multiple SAP ERP systems that can, for example, migrate one system after the other to unlock AI for the rest," he said. "In the end, to get the benefit you have to start a RISE with SAP migration. Therefore, the connector doesn't make sense for the majority of SME customers. From my perspective, this approach works only for large customers with multiple ERP systems, for example, if they take one system, move it to the cloud, and then another one. Then they can use AI, because they reach the needed ratio to use the on-prem connector. That is more or less a commercial approach. We need a solution for all customers, inde

item.title: UK MPs want AI watchdog with power to pull the plug on dangerous models
item.description: UK MPs want a watchdog with the power to pull the plug on dangerous AI models, rather than leave the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic to decide when they've gone too far. In a report shared with The Register ahead of publication on Wednesday, a parliamentary committee is calling for an AI Safety and Security Bill that would give a watchdog powers to intervene while models are still being developed. It could halt high-risk training and testing, block deployments, or suspend AI services if the risks can't be contained. LLMs are trained on billions of learned parameters and so developers can't always predict what a model will do in every situation. The recommendations come from Parliament's Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee, which questioned researchers, former AI employees, and representatives from OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Anthropic, and Meta. All four companies assured MPs they wouldn't release models they considered unsafe. The trouble is, they don't use the same yardstick for safety, and UK law doesn't generally require them to get an independent opinion before releasing anything. "We cannot give today’s AI leaders unfettered freedom to behave like modern-day Dr Frankensteins, creating dangers beyond anyone’s control," said committee chair Liam Byrne MP. Just as with aviation, pharma or nuclear safety, UK government want to rely on manufacturers' assurance alone, and want regulation. "Our hearings exposed gaps in independent scrutiny, incident reporting and powers to stop unsafe systems. Once some models are released, they cannot reliably be recalled," added Byrne. "Protection must begin while systems are being built and tested." The committee's report, Guardrails for Growth: Making AI Safe, identifies ten holes in Britain's approach to AI safety, including the lack of mandatory incident reporting, limited access for independent testers, and inadequate protections for whistleblowers. The UK already has an AI Security Institute (AISI), which has made a name for itself testing some of the world's most powerful models, but its work depends on voluntary cooperation, and it has no authority to stop a company releasing a model that raises safety concerns. MPs want AISI to continue its testing work while a separate regulator takes responsibility for enforcement. Developers of designated high-risk systems would have to provide evidence supporting their safety claims and give independent researchers access to examine them. Significant changes to a model's capabilities or safeguards would trigger further scrutiny. Former AI employees also told MPs that raising safety concerns can come at a price. Restrictive contracts, commercial pressures, and financial disincentives can all discourage staff from speaking out, the committee heard. MPs want stronger legal protections for whistleblowers and compulsory reporting of AI incidents and near misses. There's a fair bit of money riding on this, too. item.title: Tochukwu Ekoh: What My Friend’s Passing Taught Me About Kindness
item.description: A thoughtful young woman sits in a relaxed pose in a serene bedroom, reflecting peacefully. Photo credit: Alex Green/Pexels. I lost someone recently, and since then, I have found myself revisiting little moments, conversations and encounters I probably would not have given much thought to otherwise. We weren’t particularly close , or I wouldn’t describe our relationship that way . We had reconnected after a long time and started seeing each other more often, especially after I resumed work following an accident I was involved in. He gradually became part of my daily routine. Whenever I went to work, he would come to pick me up from the office, and we would go home together. In many ways, he looked out for me and made sure I got home safely. We started talking more. We would discuss life, share experiences and occasionally open up about things happening in our individual lives. There was also an emotional dimension to our friendship. He was interested in me romantically, I realised, but I didn’t feel the same way. I tried to understand my feelings, but the truth was that I simply wasn’t in love with him. I couldn’t manufacture feelings that weren’t there. Then I heard that he passed away. My first reaction, strangely, was guilt. I began asking myself: Was I a good friend to him? Was I kind enough? Was I considerate? Did I treat him well? Could I have done something differently? I caught myself wondering whether I should have given him a chance . Perhaps I should have allowed him to love me. But then would I have done that out of genuine affection or simply out of pity? And would that have been fair to either of us? My understanding is that not returning someone’s romantic feelings does not mean we cannot offer them genuine friendship, kindness and compassion. I didn’t owe him romantic love, but I could have been a good friend. That has stayed with me. Beyond the guilt, there was another question I couldn’t get out of my head: Why did God allow us to reconnect? Why, after such a long time, did our paths have to cross again? Why did we have to start talking, sharing experiences and becoming familiar with each other again, only for him to die shortly afterwards? Why him? Why at that particular time? What was the reason for that reconnection, and why did it have to end this way? The timing of certain events leaves you with more questions than answers. What makes this loss even more difficult to comprehend is how it happened. I had been the one who suffered an accident, yet I survived and was gradually recovering. He wasn’t sick. He hadn’t been involved in an accident. He simply slipped and fell, sustained an injury, and bled out. His body was not discovered until three days later. Three days. The loneliness he must have experienced within those three days, the possibility that he needed someone, and the heartbreaking thought that nobody knew what had happened to him. I cannot fully comprehend it. It also made me confront something I had perhaps never

item.title: Time for frustrated M365 customers to stage a 'distributed denial of satisfaction' action
item.description: I briefly helped with Microsoft Australia’s PR efforts in the early 2000s, when IE 6 and Windows were so bug-prone they essentially represented a welcome mat for hackers and required a deluge of patches admins couldn’t handle. Microsoft responded to that mess with a message about security being a shared responsibility involving people, process, and technology. A quarter of a century later, Microsoft’s business practices still make its customers reluctantly share the cost of its failings – most recently last week’s massive M365 outage. To protest that mess, Microsoft customers should create a new cloudy meltdown – on the pages the software giant uses to process applications for compensation after it fails to meet service level agreements. Yes, you read that right: “applications.” When Microsoft experiences an outage, customers must apply to get the service credits they’re entitled by finding the “Outage ID” related to each incident. The application page is buried deep in the Microsoft 365 Admin Center and the Outage ID is recorded elsewhere. Microsoft appears not to offer a facility for bulk uploads, so the channel partners who manage so many M365 implementations have extra work to do. That’s outrageous because the implicit promise of the cloud is that it delivers more value for less effort. Yet Microsoft requires users to do extra work to seek redress for its mistakes. Cloud also delivers fat profits for investors. Which is probably why Microsoft, which can clearly bill its customers regularly and reliably and therefore knows which services they use, hasn’t done the work to link its uptime meters and billing systems so it can automate crediting customers after outages. I understand Microsoft thinks AI is quite good at that sort of integration. Maybe its enormously reduced workforce will need it to get the job done. But rather than vibe-coding its way out of this, decency demands Microsoft quickly decide that all users impacted by last week’s automatically receive service credits, rather than asking them apply for their entitlements. If Microsoft doesn’t get proactive, the magnitude of this outage represents a moment in which its customers can show the software giant it must do better – perhaps by filing so many applications for credit that managers who oversee Redmond’s systems and finances can’t help but notice a spike of activity. Thinks of this as a distributed denial of satisfaction attack signaling that Microsoft can't solve this particular outage with a glib apology and a blog post. ®

item.title: A Chinese bottle-cap manufacturer brilliantly deflated AI hype
item.description: Shanghai is one of the world’s largest and busiest cities but is surprisingly quiet . Electric automobiles cruise silently, chased by hushed flocks of electric scooters. When I visited in early November to attend the local edition of the AI Engineer conference, I found China's attitude to AI is also quite relaxed. That's not to say interest in the topic is low, but I didn't perceive any anxious artificial-general-intelligence-is-coming-and-will-destroy-us vibe. The only conference talk that referenced AGI came from Ying Yang, a neuroscience PhD and serious influencer who has over 3.4 million followers on Chinese micro-blogging service Weibo , who enthused about the marketing and product development opportunities opening up to those who prepare for what’s coming. AGI isn't P(doom) for the Chinese AI practitioners I met; it's a great new marketing tool. Some of this may be due to the fact that the major US model makers like OpenAI, Anthropic and Google are effectively inaccessible on the Chinese side of the Great Firewall. Engineers in China use DeepSeek or Kimi or GLM or MiniMax or MiMo or Qwen, all of which are now more than good enough for almost any task, and all offered without reference to The Terminator . That's not to say that Chinese engineers and designers aren't facing the same crisis of self-worth we've seen elsewhere. A spectacular keynote from Ryo Lu asked, "When we can do anything, do we still know what we want?" Are our measures of self-worth pointless when we can no longer prove who we are by how many lines of code we've written, or frameworks we've designed? Ryo landed on a line I'm hearing more frequently: "I want to build tools to help me be more and more involved, not prove that I'm needed less and less." What followed showed just how good that tooling has become and what an AI engineer can do with it. I saw an impressive demo from AutoArk of a 35 billion-parameter model running in just 2.5GB of smartphone RAM on an iPhone 16 Pro. DYNA 's Zhong Shen showed how it builds robot hardware that will work with AI models updating every month. My favorite presentation came from a bottle cap manufacturer called named Zhu Shihui, who reminded everyone in the audience that “the last mile is half the journey.” Zhu flayed the class of consultants who never realize some manufacturing equipment is pre-digital but still insist every process can be easily automated. Never mind that workers in those factories lack deep digital skills (Zhu's average employee is in their late 40s) and that companies of this sort operate on margins so thin that resources simply aren't available to mount a complete transformation. Instead of swinging in on an AI wrecking ball, Zhu suggested the best approach is to exercise humility by seeking out an organization's tacit knowledge and using that as the basis for transformation. Not long after Zhu left the podium, one of my Australian fellow travelers noted the significant proportion of women at the conference. I hadn

item.title: Temu's compliance regime is low-quality, fits badly, and full of holes, says Europe
item.description: Chinese e-tailer Temu has a reputation for selling low-quality knockoff products at low prices made possible through use of forced labor. Now, the European Commission has made a preliminary finding that the company also runs a low-quality compliance regime that means it’s not meeting its regulatory obligations. The Commission issued that finding yesterday, accusing Temu of breaching its Digital Services Act (DSA) obligation to operate serious measures that mitigate the risk of illegal products being offered on its platform. Temu is a marketplace that allows third parties to sell on its platform, a model that doesn’t relieve it of responsibility for the goods available on its site and apps. Eurocrats therefore have beef with Temu over several matters, including: Requiring sellers who use the platform to test the quality of “only a very small share of products,” and then often not bothering to check the reports; Not doing enough to prioritize checks of products in known high risk categories, like toys and cosmetics, then not following up on those checks; Running a moderation system that mostly considers whether products comply with Temu’s terms and conditions, rather than product safety; Not hiring enough human moderators to keep pace with growth in listings on Temu; When it finds stores selling non-compliant goods, Temu acts against that store – but not the trader who may sell the same products in multiple stores; Allowing stores to commit many serious infringements, including selling products that fail safety checks, before suspending their stores. A Temu spokesperson told The Register the company respectfully disagrees with the EC's findings. "Temu invests significantly in compliance infrastructure and human expertise and implements a suite of control measures that effectively mitigate illegal product risks with a consistently low incidence of problematic products," the spokesperson said. "We will review and respond to the preliminary findings carefully and will continue to engage constructively with the Commission. We are confident that we will reach an amicable resolution of the matter that fully addresses the Commission's remaining concerns." The EC has already tangled with Temu. In 2024 Eurocrats investigated its risk assessment processes. In May 2026, Eurocrats found Temu’s processes inadequate and levied a €200 million fine. Brussels also sent a €550 million fine to another Chinese e-tailer, Alibaba, for not doing enough to stop the sale of dangerous goods. This announcement of new action against Temu invoked Article 35 of the Digital Services Act, the sweeping regulation of online businesses under which the EU could fine Temu up to six percent of its global revenue and order corrective actions. Europe is concerned that the low prices Chinese e-tailers charge are enabled by forced labor and ignoring dangerous products. EC officials believe those practices mean the likes of Temu don’t compete on a level playing field with continental retail

item.title: Oracle reveals fix-this-ASAP-grade Java4Shell bug that allows attacks on many third-party apps
item.description: The United States Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has urged Java users to immediately patch a high-severity flaw in the software, which attackers can use to crash the Java virtual machine or achieve unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE). Oracle revealed the flaw in its monthly patch dump for November , which offers 655 patches, 62 of them rated critical, affecting 62 products. Several of the flaws are rated more dangerous than the Java problem, CVE-2026-114938 , which Big Red didn’t single out as worthy of special attention despite CISA’s warning . The cyber-agency’s decision seems apt because vulnerability research and red teaming outfit Calif.io, which discovered the flaw, used its X account to claim news of the problem had leaked before public disclosure and the release of Oracle's fixes. By then, Calif had already tested the flaw, which it named “Java4Shell,” and found applications including Keycloak, Atlassian’s Jira and Confluence, Jenkins, Apache Kafka Broker, and Elasticsearch are susceptible to RCE. Calif, which also helped to find the PHP2Shell flaw , says the flaw is a memory-corruption vulnerability in OpenJDK's Base64 decoder. “Base64 is a very common way of representing binary data as text. It is used in authentication protocols, to encode file uploads, and to deliver network messages,” the company explained. “To decode Base64 faster, OpenJDK uses specialized x86-64 CPU instructions to process many bytes at once.” “We discovered a bug in that optimized machine-level code that lets malformed input overwrite neighboring memory. With careful exploitation, the corruption can reveal sensitive memory, as Heartbleed did, or lead to remote code execution. The corruption itself can be triggered by just 64 A characters followed by a single =:” Calif applied the CVSS 4.0 bug-rating scheme and gave the flaw a critical-rated score of 9.2/10. Infosec outfit SentinelOne’s analysis suggests the flaw “sits in the Java standard library, so exploit traffic is specific to each application.” “Any Base64 value an application passes to java.util.Base64.Decoder can carry the payload, including HTTP Basic credentials, SAML artifacts, CSRF tokens, and MIME encoded words. In default configurations of the affected applications listed above, attackers can reach this code path prior to authentication.” Cisco’s Talos security team pointed out that the flaw is present in OpenJDK Java versions 17.0.6 and later running on x86-64 CPUs with AVX-512 VBMI (Vector Byte Manipulation Instructions) support enabled. “These vulnerabilities have already been tested against a suite of Java applications with success, but the attack surface is likely much larger as additional targets are tested and confirmed,” Talos advised. Cisco’s infosec experts urged adoption of the fixed versions of Java Oracle posted on Tuesday but noted it is possible to mitigate the flaw on x86-64 machines by starting the JVM with support for AVX-512 disabled. Akamai’s Chief

The announcement is a striking inversion of how we've traditionally used software. Rather than an app like Word being the attraction and Clippy the assistant to help you use it, Microsoft envisions the new Copilot integrations will see agents driving things, with the software packages riding shotgun. Applications will become plugin components of the agent's work, backed by an organizational knowledge layer that draws context from emails, meetings, calendars, chats, and files. Users will now be able to create documents, spreadsheets, and presentations directly in Copilot, with the resulting files remaining editable in their respective Office applications. item.title: Daily disruptive outages that ground planes and halt work – welcome to the new normal
item.description: Another day, another disruptive network outage (or two) as government officials and company execs scramble to assure an anxious populace that these are not coordinated cyberattacks – and security experts call this the new normal. A classified network that the US National Security Agency uses for internal communications, called NSANet, went offline on Tuesday in what the agency described as a “temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance.” “While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues,” the NSA said in a statement following media reports about the outage. “NSA's infrastructure is designed with multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events.” Around the same time, Apple users began reporting issues across multiple services – including Apple Support, iCloud, the App Store, Apple Pay, and more – with Apple retail stores worldwide also reportedly experiencing disruptions that halted sales and in-person support. A day earlier, customers at major US banks including JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, and US Bank reported service outages that Chase attributed to “a software bug in on-premise hardware systems - there is no evidence this is cyber-related.” All of these high-profile outages followed last week’s US Federal Aviation Authority (FAA) order g rounding all planes on Friday due to problems with copper wiring during an L3Harris network upgrade, and a Microsoft 365 outage on Thursday. Redmond later blamed the massive service disruption on a faulty software update it pushed back in July. Despite the weekend respite from network outages, your humble vulture still had to field is-this-the-beginning-of-the-end questions from friends and family all day Saturday and Sunday, most of whom suspected Russia or China – maybe even Iran – caused the spate of downed systems and services. A highly sophisticated, coordinated nation-state hack would be a much more exciting cause for the disruptions. The real culprit, however, appears to be aging, under-funded infrastructure , riddled with decades-old bugs and held together by digital sticks and glue . “As someone who started out as a hacker , I know how tempting it is to connect the dots when major systems fail one after another,” Remedio CEO Tal Kollender told The Register, adding that there’s “no credible public evidence that these outages were part of a coordinated cyberattack,” and most have been attributed to technical failures. “What concerns me more is what these incidents reveal about the fragility of our digital infrastructure. We've built an interconnected world on layers of aging systems, complex configurations, and dependencies that organizations don't always fully understand. A single misconfiguration, failed update, or broken dependency can create disruption on a massive scale, even without an attacker,” Kollender said. “The uncomfor

item.title: GPU giants throw HPC users some tasty crumbs
item.description: At Supercomputing 2026 this week, Nvidia unveiled a new variant of its Rubin GPUs aimed at – you’ll never believe it – high performance computing (HPC). The creatively named Rubin HPC promises more than 50,000 CUDA cores, nearly twice that of the AI-focused version of the chip that Nvidia unveiled earlier this year. It will arrive sometime in 2028. According to Dan Ernst, Nvidia’s senior director of supercomputing, the new chip offers a rebalanced architecture optimized for the kinds of simulation, engineering, and high-performance analytics workloads common in the HPC and scientific computing communities. This is not the first time Nvidia has introduced specialized hardware. Last year, the company optimized its B300 accelerator for AI inferencing workloads. “Rubin HPC is the same idea,” Ernst told El Reg . “Within the Rubin platform, but we’re building variants to really focus on a specific sub domain of applications.” Details remain remarkably thin. Nvidia hasn’t disclosed peak performance memory capacity or bandwidth. That said, the chip will likely include features which show Nvidia can think beyond AI and still cares about the HPC community. Fearing that Nvidia could ignore HPC is reasonable becuase beginning with the launch of Blackwell Ultra (B300/GB300), the company traded double-precision matrix acceleration for higher throughput at lower-precisions. The result was a chip that at FP4 churned out 15 petaFLOPS of AI compute, but just 1.3 teraFLOPS at FP64. That's good for AI, but less useful for scientists. When Nvidia unveiled Rubin, it seemed the GPU-slinger would continue this trend. At 33 teraFLOPS, the chip was not only slower at FP64 than the Blackwell GPUs it replaced, but slower than Nvidia’s now four-year-old Hopper accelerators as well. Nvidia contended that for sparse vector-heavy workloads measured by the High Performance Conjugate Gradients (HPCG) benchmark, the higher ratio of memory bandwidth to compute should deliver meaningful performance gains. Meanwhile, for dense matrix-heavy workloads, for which benchmarks like High-Performance Linpack (HPL) are representative, Nvidia adopted a new strategy: FP64 emulation. We discussed the pros and cons of this technique in greater detail earlier this year, but in a nutshell it uses an algorithm derived from the so-called Ozaki Scheme. The algorithm works by decomposing FP64 matrix operations into a string of INT8 operations that, when run on Nvidia’s tensor cores, achieve higher-than-native performance. Nvidia, we’re told, isn’t using INT8, but it is unlocking substantial performance gains, at least for certain workloads. According to Nvidia, Rubin can churn out up to 200 emulated FP64 matrix teraFLOPS. While Ernst didn’t offer any specifics, he assured us that Nvidia’s HPC hardware should offer native FP64 matrix performance and customers won't have to rely entirely on emulation. Assessing the new chip's vector performance is much easier. With more than 50 thousand CUDA cores (by ou

item.title: NASA's Voyager 1 launched second, so how did it beat Voyager 2 to a light-day by nearly a decade?
item.description: null Voyager 1 is about to reach a light-day of distance in space, but Voyager 2 won't hit the mark until about 2035. Why the big difference? On Nov. 18, Voyager 1 will be so far away from Earth that it will take a full light-day (24 hours) to send a signal to the distant spacecraft, at 16,094,799,096 miles (25,902,068,356 kilometers). Since light is essentially the maximum speed in the universe (absent using devices like wormholes, or quantum-physics puzzles), it's a big deal — so big that NASA will be celebrating the milestone by asking fans to shine Morse Code signals at the sky. But why will Voyager 2 take nearly a decade longer? It comes down to choices made for speed and science during the twin missions' nearly 50-year journey, specifically during the first bit when they were flying by planets. The result is Voyager 1 is zooming out at a speed of 3.5 Earth-sun distances (astronomical units a year), while Voyager 2 has a more stately speed of 3.1 Earth-sun distances, according to NASA . Need for speed The original aim of both the spacecraft, which launched about two weeks apart in 1977 with Voyager 2 going first, was to look at Jupiter and Saturn. If funding persisted, which it did, the hope was to bring Voyager 2 past Uranus and Neptune, taking advantage of a rare planetary alignment. Voyager 1, by contrast, made a turn at Saturn to look at the planet's rings and the prebiotic (pre-life-chemistry) moon of Titan , before flying outside the plane of the solar system. NASA had a range of trajectory options to consider when launching the spacecraft, and elected to bring Voyager 1 at a faster trajectory — as illustrated in this video by Britannica, where you can quickly see the spacecraft overtaking Voyager 2 on its way to Jupiter even though Voyager 1. Voyager 1 arrived at Jupiter on March 5, 1979 while Voyager 2 got there four months later on July 9. The trajectories of Voyager 1 and 2 through the outer solar system. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech) Each of the spacecraft then performed a "gravity assist"—a sort of slingshot around the planet in which they took a tiny bit of momentum from Jupiter to gain speed as the spacecraft flew to Saturn. This technique is used constantly, such as recently when the ESCAPADE Mars mission flew two spacecraft by Earth on the way to the Red Planet, as it allows spacecraft to gain speed while saving on fuel. The planets themselves don't slow down that much. "Because the planet is so much more massive than the spacecraft, the transfer doesn't affect the planet to any measurable extent, but to the spacecraft it's a big deal," the Planetary Society wrote . "For example, we can calculate that during the Voyager encounters with Jupiter in 1979, Jupiter slowed down by roughly 10 to the -24th power kilometers per second — a change much too small to measure." "But each Voyager gained about 10 km/s [6.2 miles/s], a pretty big number," the society continued about the Jupiter encounter. This was "enough to put them on a

item.title: Satya sorry for SaaS-y SNAFU - look over there, more AI!
item.description: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella's Ignite conference keynote on Tuesday was all about trust. He opened by promising to earn back trust after last week's massive M365 outage and went on to focus on the need for organizations to trust their AI models. "So last week in some sense was really a reminder of how critical digital infrastructure is as the dial tone for the world," said Nadella. "We know the trust you place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously. And in that context, I know we have work to do to provide that resilience that you can count on, the world can count on, and we are committed to ensuring that we learn and we continuously improve." Speaking at San Francisco's Moscone Center, Nadella described three areas of focus for the company as it works to build what he referred to as a frontier ecosystem: "Keeping the human at the center of it all, ensuring that you have ownership over your organization's intelligence and learning, and trust." Anthrocentrism is a tough sell just weeks after offering buyouts to 60,000 employees . Describing the shift from hand-written code to agent-written code, Nadella suggested developers have moved from building software artifacts to building software factories that build those artifacts. "The important thing here though is to remember still that that human intent, that judgment, that experience, skills, expertise all very much matter," he said. People may judge development work, but ask them whether they have the same sense of ownership as when they wrote every line. As to ensuring that organizations have ownership over their intelligence, that borders on heresy for a company with massive cloud computing commitments specifically to run AI workloads. If everyone really owned their machine learning models and ran them in their own data centers and on employee computers, Azure would be in trouble. Yet Nadella emphasized ownership – which isn't at all obvious given the legal ambiguity of who owns AI generated code and whether it can be copyrighted . "In the age of AI, the key question is how do individual firms continually build and own their learning and tacit knowledge?" he said. "For an economy to remain an economy where many firms exist and thrive, intelligence by definition needs to be broadly distributed versus just collapsed into a couple of models." Suffice to say that Nadella is promoting client control over AI data that's processed mostly on equipment rented from Microsoft, with some allowance for customer-controlled infrastructure. But that still ought to concern frontier AI labs like Anthropic and OpenAI that favor a white-glove, black-box service model where they are the arbiters of access. As for the third pillar of Nadella's vision, that's trust, which remains missing in action. "How can you even trust all this powerful technology?" Nadella asked. item.title: Jensen Huang thrilled to be spending time with family, but will retake leadership burden if Nvidia asks
item.description: No surprises here. Ex-Nvidia boss Jensen Huang says that he'd be willing to come back to the company he founded, if the board wants him to return. In Huang’s first public comments since his resignation last week over a series of extramarital affairs, both with Nvidia staff and an alleged Chinese spy at one of its customers, he admits that he may have made life hard for the company he spent 33 years building, but he’s really sorry…and Nvidia couldearn really use him. “I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life,” Huang admitted. “I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation.” But soft, what open letter through yonder news cycle break? It's one calling widely for Huang’s return – and he's happy to oblige if Nvidia’s post-Jensen crisis-mode leadership is willing to indulge him. “Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO,” Huang said. “Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics.” Nvidia, Huang added, has been his life’s work, and is a “once-in-a-generation company” that perhaps needs his steady hand at the helm. There have been a number of public calls for Huang’s return to the head of the company he helped create, from tech industry heavyweights and Nvidia shareholders like Elon Musk, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan, as well as a number of current Nvidia employees, company partners, and shareholders upset that the stock has lost more than a quarter of its value since reports of the affair first emerged. One petition pleading for his return has nearly 200,000 signatures . Faced with that, what else can a disgraced billionaire tech founder who may have literally have been in bed with a Chinese spy do? Duty calls. “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” Huang said. Reports citing Nvidia insiders with knowledge of the matter suggest the board isn’t considering reinstating Huang as CEO despite the public push. On the company's third-quarter earnings call late Tuesday, new board chairman Harvey Jones said that Huang's behavior was "Inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards and cultural norms” and that the board "does not expect to reinstate him as CEO," putting a seeming end to the question. item.title: Space is filling up with junk. Could laser-reflecting mirrors help humanity clean things up?
item.description: null A British startup thinks it can help humanity deal with its space junk problem. Millions of pieces of space debris circle Earth at the moment, according to the European Space Agency (ESA). Even the smallest fragments are potentially dangerous, given how fast stuff travels in orbit. Experts have proposed a range of measures to deal with this junk. The smallest bits, for example, may require big space nets, or lasering the stuff down to Earth. Large satellites are increasingly being deliberately deorbited these days, and a few have even been refueled to keep them operating in orbit — something that will likely start happening more and more over the coming years. Now, the British startup Foundational has another idea to throw into the mix: retroreflectors. The company argues that its tech can help fight the space-junk problem — and it just proved out a demo version in an orbital test. London-based Foundational recently tested its Retro-2 laser retroreflector system, which it developed in collaboration with ESA. The early-stage test was designed to ensure that Foundational's retroreflectors can return laser-ranging signals from a satellite , at altitudes between about 600 kilometers and 870 kilometers (about 370 to 540 miles), with a usable range distance of 300 to 1,400 km (186 to 870 miles). The long-term aim is to create a sort of tracking device for spacecraft, so they can be monitored in orbit even after they fall silent. Foundational's Retro-2 retroreflector, which is designed to help trackers keep tabs on satellites in orbit. It recently passed its first in-space test. (Image credit: Foundational) The tech, Foundational said in a statement today (Nov. 17), needs "no electronics, power or commands from its host spacecraft" and allows ground stations to keep tabs on the orbiting spacecraft. The demo mission launched this past July on SpaceX's Transporter-17 rideshare flight. It attached Retro-2 — a mini device with seven reflectors — to a small satellite that was integrated into an ION carrier craft operated by the Italian company D-Orbit. Retro-2 worked as advertised, successfully returning 6,111 laser shots beamed from the from the ground across five passes in low Earth orbit . "Our tests have shown that a device weighing just 50 grams [1.8 ounces] can deliver millimeter-level ranging precision," Dave Gooding, Foundational's co-founder and chief technical officer, said in today's statement. "As space becomes increasingly crowded, keeping satellites trackable throughout their lifetime and beyond is critical to managing collision risks." Foundational's Retro-2 retroreflector is seen before its July 2026 launch. The device is attached to its cubesat, which itself is integrated into one of D-Orbit's ION carrier craft. (Image credit: Foundational) Foundational is in its early stages — it was founded in 2025 and just emerged from stealth last month. Nevertheless the company has already raised £8.2 million ($10.9 million) in pre-seed funding. Fo

item.title: Python parallel debugging comes to HPC thanks to TotalView upgrade
item.description: The OG debugger for supercomputer iron has buddied up with the data-science darling now muscling in on HPC: Python. At the SC26 supercomputing show this week (booth #2829), Perforce Software is demonstrating how its TotalView parallel debugging tool now understands Python, easing the path for using the language on large, distributed apps, particularly those in the high-performance computing (HPC) space. In the HPC community, "Python has grown in popularity,” said Bill Burns , Perforce vice president of software engineering, in an interview with The Register . TotalView is a debugger specializing in picking apart parallel applications for developers. Built in the late 1980s for military applications, TotalView today largely serves developers in high-performance computing (HPC), where large scientific applications are spread across multiple servers, running in parallel on thousands or even tens of thousands of processes. (Perforce acquired TotalView in 2019 in its purchase of the DevOps-focused Rogue Wave Software.) To date, TotalView has supported C/C++ and Fortran. With the latest quarterly release, the tool now supports Python as well. Debugging a thousand cores C/C++ has long had a decent dedicated debugger in GDB , but figuring out what went wrong across multiple threads is a special kind of torture. Each thread needs to be instrumented, and all the output needs to be aggregated and filtered to just highlight the interesting stuff. Regular debuggers get overwhelmed with all this info. “Even if you have 10,000 things going on, if you have one crash in there, TotalView can pinpoint that,” Burns said. It can look at the state of the process, the threads within that process or the GPU that process is using. In the HPC space, computing work has traditionally been written in C/C++. And at least some HPC iron still runs Fortran . Thanks to it being easy to learn and use, Python has gained a foothold in this community as well. The mpi4py library bridges a Python program to the Message Passing Interface (MPI), allowing different parts of an application running on different hardware to communicate. Python became more amenable to parallel programming at the thread level with version 3.14, released a year ago , which included the ability to use concurrent interpreters, as well as the long-awaited free threading support, thanks to the disabling of the global interpreter lock (GIL). “If you have a CPU with 64 cores, you can run 64 independent threads all working in unison on that CPU. Without GIL, those threads will run fully asynchronously,” Burns said. Multinode scientific simulations, distributed AI training, and large applications that would benefit from shared memory have all become fair game for Python. Of course, with 500 or 1,000 interpreters all running in parallel, debugging will also get more difficult. “Now you're going to end up with lock and thread contention and race conditions and all the things that C++ and Fortran developers have dealt wit
